lessons.title: Direct indexing with array address arithmetic
lessons.summary: Address arithmetic gives direct access to a fixed-width slot.
lessons.body:
An **array** is the simplest data structure there is: a fixed number of same-sized slots laid out one after another in memory. Almost every other structure in this course is either built on arrays or defined by how it differs from one.

Two properties make arrays special:

- **Contiguous layout.** Element at the next index sits immediately after its predecessor. There are no gaps and no pointers between them.
- **Uniform element size.** Every slot is the same number of bytes, so the machine can compute where any element lives.

Everything good about arrays (instant indexing, cache-friendliness) and everything bad (expensive inserts, fixed size) follows from those two facts.

## Indexing is arithmetic

Memory is a long row of numbered bytes; the number of a byte is its **memory address**. To read element `i`, the machine needs that element's address. Because the slots are contiguous and all the same size, it can work the address out directly from where the array starts:

```formula essential
address(i) = base + i × size
where
address(i): the memory address of the first byte of element i
i: the index of the element you want, counting from 0
base: the memory address where the array starts (the address of element 0)
size: how many bytes one element takes, e.g. 4 for a 32-bit integer, 8 for a 64-bit float or a pointer
In words: skip over i whole elements from the start of the array; the element you want begins right there.
```

The formula only works because every slot is the same size and there are no gaps; a structure without those two properties (a linked list, for example) has no such shortcut.

That is one multiply and one add, whatever the array's length. This is why indexing is **O(1)**, or **constant time**: the cost does not grow as the array gets longer. The CPU does not walk to element `i`, it calculates where it is.

```
int32: 4-byte slots, start address 1000

index:    0     1     2     3     4
        +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
        |  7  | 12  |  3  | 40  |  9  |
        +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
addr:   1000  1004  1008  1012  1016
```

In the drawing, element 3 starts twelve bytes after the start: three whole 4-byte slots are skipped. Element 0 is zero elements past `base`, which is why most languages start indexing at **0**: the index is an *offset* from the start.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Houses on equal-width plots
> Imagine a new street where every plot is exactly 10 metres wide and the plots are numbered from 0 at the corner. To find house number 7 you do not walk past houses 0 to 6 counting front doors; you measure 70 metres from the corner.
>
> **How it maps:** The corner is `base`, the plot width is the element `size` and the house number is the index `i`. Measuring straight to the plot is the multiply-and-add that makes indexing O(1).
>
> **Where it stops:** Memory addresses count bytes, and the machine computes the address rather than travelling anywhere. The shortcut also depends on every slot having the same width: a street with mixed plot sizes, like a list of variable-length records, would need a separate table of positions.

> [!note] O(1) access, O(n) search
> For an array of n elements: indexing by position is O(1). Finding a *value* in an unsorted array is still O(n) (**linear time**: the work grows in proportion to n), because you must look at each slot. If the array is sorted, binary search finds a value in O(log n), where log n means log₂ n, the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1 (about 20 for a million elements).

## Key takeaways
- Address arithmetic gives direct access to a fixed-width slot.
- Position lookup and searching for an unsorted value are different operations.

## Further reading
- [Array (data structure) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_(data_structure))

questions.prompt: Array `small` holds 1,000 four-byte integers and array `big` holds 1,000,000. Both are ordinary contiguous arrays. How does the cost of reading `big[999999]` compare with reading `small[999]`?

options.text: About the same: each read is one address calculation, whatever the array's length
options.explanation: Correct. The address is the start address plus the index times the element size. That is one multiply and one add for either array, so position lookup is O(1).

options.text: About 1,000 times slower, because `big` is 1,000 times longer
options.explanation: This treats indexing as walking from the start. A linked list works that way; an array computes the slot's address directly.

options.text: Slower only if `big[999998]` has not been read first
options.explanation: Reading an element never depends on visiting its neighbour. Earlier reads can affect cache behaviour, but not the number of steps needed to find the address.

options.text: Slightly slower, in proportion to the logarithm of the length, as in binary search
options.explanation: Binary search finds a *value* in sorted data. Reading by *position* needs no search at all.

questions.workedExample:
1. An array's slots are contiguous and all the same size, so the machine finds element `i` by starting at the array's base address and skipping `i` whole slots.
2. That is one multiply (index times element size) and one add (plus the base), for both arrays. Neither calculation looks at any other element.
3. So the number of steps does not grow with the array's length: indexing is O(1), constant time.
4. Contrast: finding the *value* 42 in an unsorted array is O(n), because you may have to check every slot. Position lookup and value search are different operations.
5. Real timings can still differ slightly because of caching (covered next), but that is a hardware effect, not extra steps in the lookup.

lessons.title: Cache locality and row-major grids
lessons.summary: Scan the contiguous dimension for sequential memory access.
lessons.body:
The preceding unit derived an address from the array base, index and fixed slot size. Constant-time indexing is a data-structure model; memory locality explains why two scans that do the same number of operations can still differ in real elapsed time.

## Why contiguous memory is fast

Both indexed access and a single pointer load are constant-time operations in the usual RAM model. Their measured latencies can differ because that model abstracts away the memory hierarchy.

CPUs do not fetch single bytes from RAM. They transfer a whole **cache line** (its size depends on the processor; this lesson assumes 64 bytes) and keep it in a small, fast cache. A cache hit can be much faster than a main-memory access. The actual latencies depend on the hardware, contention and access pattern, so no universal nanosecond figures are quoted here.

When you scan an array, one aligned 64-byte cache line contains sixteen 4-byte integers. A hardware **prefetcher** can recognise a sequential pattern and fetch later lines ahead of demand; effectiveness depends on the processor, stride and workload. This is **spatial locality**, and it is why a simple loop over an array is one of the fastest things a computer can do.

A linked list (covered later in this module) scatters its nodes around the heap. Each step can be a cache miss. Scanning n elements is O(n) for both on paper; dependent pointer loads can make the list slower, but no speed ratio follows without measuring the workload.

### 2D arrays: row-major order

A rectangular C or C++ array such as `int grid[3][4]` is contiguous and row-major: row 0 first, then row 1. A newly created C-order NumPy array has this layout too; NumPy also supports other strides and orders. Java int[][] is an array of references to separate int[] rows, which may have different lengths. Fortran, MATLAB and R normally use column-major layout.

```
grid (3 x 4), row-major:

[r0c0 r0c1 r0c2 r0c3 r1c0 r1c1 ...]
```

To locate a row-and-column element, count complete earlier rows and then the earlier slots in its row:

```formula reference
address(r, c) = base + (r × cols + c) × size
where
address(r, c): the memory address of the element in row r, column c
r: the row number, counting from 0
c: the column number, counting from 0
cols: how many columns each row has (4 in the grid above)
base: the memory address of element (0, 0), where the grid starts
size: how many bytes one element takes
In words: to reach a cell in a row-major grid, skip every complete earlier row, then the earlier cells in its own row, and convert that count of elements into bytes. Moving one column along moves one element; moving one row down jumps a whole row.
```

In the 3-by-4 grid of 4-byte integers above, row 1, column 2 comes after six earlier cells, so it starts twenty-four bytes after the grid's start. In a column-major language the roles swap: you skip whole columns first.

Loop order matters. Iterating row by row walks memory sequentially. Iterating column by column jumps a whole row's worth of bytes (the column count multiplied by the element size) every step, potentially touching a different cache line each time when that **stride** is large. Performance depends on dimensions, cache hierarchy and compiler transformations.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Reading a page across or down
> A printed page is laid out line by line. Reading across each line uses every word your eyes land on before you move down. Reading only the first word of every line, then the second word of every line, makes your eyes jump a whole line each time and revisit the page many times.
>
> **How it maps:** The page is row-major memory, a line of text is a row, and each glance is a cache line: it brings in a run of neighbouring elements. A row-by-row loop uses the whole glance; a column-by-column loop jumps a full row's stride and may use only one element from each line it brings in.
>
> **Where it stops:** A reader can see a whole page at once, while a cache holds a limited number of lines and may evict one before the loop comes back to it. Hardware prefetching and compiler loop interchange can also change the outcome, so the real cost must be measured.

## Key takeaways
- Scan the contiguous dimension for sequential memory access.
- A cache-performance claim needs stated hardware and workload assumptions.

## Further reading
- [Array (data structure) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_(data_structure))
- [Row- and column-major order — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Row-_and_column-major_order)

questions.prompt: In C, `double grid[4096][4096]` (128 MiB with 8-byte doubles) is summed two ways. Loop A iterates `for r ... for c ... grid[r][c]`; loop B swaps the loops: `for c ... for r ... grid[r][c]`. Both do 16.7 million additions. Assuming 64-byte cache lines and no loop interchange, which access pattern is usually more cache-friendly, and why?

options.text: They take the same time; both are O(n²)
options.explanation: Both loops do the same O(n²) additions, where n is the grid's side length (4,096), but Big-O hides constant factors. Here memory access patterns differ wildly, and that can dominate running time, depending on the cache hierarchy and workload.

options.text: B, because columns are stored contiguously in C
options.explanation: That's column-major order, used by Fortran and MATLAB. C is row-major.

options.text: A, because C is row-major: A walks memory sequentially, using every byte of each cache line
options.explanation: Correct. In A, consecutive accesses are 8 bytes apart, so each 64-byte cache line serves 8 doubles and the prefetcher streams ahead. In B, each access jumps 4096 × 8 = 32 KiB, touching a new cache line almost every time.

options.text: B, because the compiler always vectorises the inner loop better
options.explanation: Vectorisation favours contiguous inner loops, which helps A, not B. Compilers can sometimes interchange loops, but you shouldn't rely on it.

questions.workedExample:
1. C is row-major, so each row's 4,096 doubles sit together. Moving one column along moves 8 bytes; moving one row down jumps a whole row of 4,096 eight-byte doubles, which is 32 KiB.
2. Loop A, inner loop over `c`: consecutive accesses are 8 bytes apart. One aligned 64-byte line serves eight consecutive doubles, and the prefetcher can stream later lines ahead. Actual misses and prefetch effectiveness depend on the cache state.
3. Loop B, inner loop over `r`: consecutive accesses are 32 KiB apart, so each one lands in a different cache line. Whether those lines survive until the next column needs them depends on cache capacity, associativity and conflicts; the access pattern alone does not fix the miss count.
4. Result: B can be much slower despite identical arithmetic; a speed ratio needs a measurement. Both loops do the same number of additions (quadratic in the side length of a square grid): Big-O counts the additions, not the cache misses.
5. Rule: make the innermost loop run along the contiguous dimension.

lessons.title: Array operations and spare capacity
lessons.summary: Interior changes shift elements; position lookup does not.
lessons.body:
An array gives direct indexed access, but its physical neighbours must move when you open or close an interior gap.

## Operations and their cost

In this table n is the number of elements in the array and i is the zero-based position being read or changed.

| Operation | Cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Read/write `a[i]` | O(1) | Address arithmetic |
| Search (unsorted) | O(n) | Check every slot |
| Insert/delete at end | O(1)* | No shifting |
| Insert/delete at `i` | O(n − i + 1) without resizing | Shift the tail; reallocation may add O(n) |

*For a dynamic array, amortised; see below.

Inserting at position `i` means shifting every later element one slot right to make room. Inserting at the front of a million-element array moves a million elements.

```python
a = [10, 20, 30, 40]
a.insert(1, 15)   # shifts 20, 30, 40 right
print(a)          # [10, 15, 20, 30, 40]
```

## Static vs dynamic arrays

A **fixed-size array** has a size chosen when it is created; this is distinct from static storage duration. C's `int a[100]` and Java's `new int[100]` are fixed-size: you cannot append a 101st element.

A **dynamic array** (resizable array) wraps a fixed-size backing array and tracks two numbers:

- **length**: how many elements are in use.
- **capacity**: how many slots the underlying array has.

When the length equals the capacity and you append, it allocates a bigger array, copies everything across, and frees the old one.

```
capacity 4, length 4: full
[ a | b | c | d ]

append e -> allocate 8, copy, add e
[ a | b | c | d | e |   |   |   ]
```

### What the Python operations touch

A CPython list’s contiguous slots hold references to objects. Indexing chooses one slot directly; membership scans values until a match or the end. An unsorted list does not get fast membership merely because its storage supports direct indexing. Equality comparisons can themselves be expensive; the linear scan bound counts comparisons, assuming each has fixed cost.

An append usually writes into spare capacity. Occasionally it reallocates the backing storage, making that individual operation linear in the current length. “Amortised constant time” describes the total cost spread across a sequence, rather than promising identical latency for every append. The next unit proves why geometric growth gives that guarantee.

Negative indices are translated relative to the stored length, so replacing the last item is still direct access. Removing the last item needs no shifting, while removing the first shifts the remaining references. CPython may also shrink its allocation on some pops; its end-pop bound is amortised.

## Key takeaways
- Interior changes shift elements; position lookup does not.
- Length counts live elements, while capacity includes spare slots.

## Further reading
- [Dynamic array — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_array)
- [Array (data structure) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_(data_structure))

questions.prompt: You have a Python list `nums` of one million **unsorted** integers. What are the costs of `nums[500000]` and `42 in nums` respectively?

options.text: O(1) and O(1)
options.explanation: Indexing is O(1), but membership in a list is not: unlike a set or dict there's no hashing, so Python has to compare against elements one by one.

options.text: O(n) and O(n)
options.explanation: This mistakes indexing for walking the list. A list is an array of pointers, so the slot is found by address arithmetic, not by stepping from the start.

options.text: O(log n) and O(n)
options.explanation: O(log n) is binary search on sorted data. Indexing by position needs no search at all.

options.text: O(1) and O(n)
options.explanation: Correct. Position lookup is one address calculation: the start of the pointer array plus 500,000 pointer slots (typically 8 bytes each on a conventional 64-bit build), O(1). `in` on an unsorted list is a linear scan, O(n) in the worst case.

questions.workedExample:
Here n is the number of elements, one million. O(1) means constant time (the cost doesn't depend on n); O(n) means the cost grows in proportion to n.

1. `nums[500000]`: CPython computes the slot address directly from the start of its pointer array. O(1).
2. `42 in nums`: the list has no index on values, so Python compares 42 with nums[0], nums[1], ... until it finds a match or reaches the end. Worst case: one million comparisons. O(n).
3. If you need fast membership tests, convert to a `set` (average O(1) per lookup, covered in the hash tables module). If the data is sorted, `bisect` gives O(log n), where log n is log₂ n: the number of halvings to get from n down to 1, about 20 for a million.

questions.prompt: Which of these Python list operations is O(n) rather than O(1) (amortised)?

options.text: `a.append(x)`
options.explanation: Append writes into spare capacity at the end. It occasionally resizes, but geometric growth makes it amortised O(1).

options.text: `a.insert(0, x)`
options.explanation: Correct. Inserting at the front shifts every existing element one slot to the right, so it costs time proportional to the list's length.

options.text: `a.pop()`
options.explanation: Popping from the end needs no shifting; CPython may occasionally shrink the backing allocation, so the guarantee is amortised.
Negative indexing is just `len(a) - 1`, still one address calculation.

questions.workedExample:
Ask of each operation: does it move other elements? (Each is applied to the original `a`.)

```
a = [A, B, C, D]

append(E):   [A, B, C, D, E]
             nothing moves
pop():       [A, B, C]
             nothing moves
insert(0,X): [X, A, B, C, D]
             A..D all shift
```

The front insert moves all n elements, where n is the list's length: O(n). If you need cheap inserts and removals at the front, use `collections.deque`.

lessons.title: Why geometric growth amortises copying
lessons.summary: Multiply capacity by a constant factor greater than one to bound total copying.
lessons.body:
A dynamic array distinguishes its live length from its backing capacity. When a full array grows, the old elements must be copied into the new block. This unit counts that copying across a long run of appends; allocation costs and allocator-specific in-place growth are outside the model.

### Why growth must be geometric

Copying n elements is O(n) work, so you might expect appends to be slow. The trick is *how much* to grow. To compare growth policies, count the total number of element copies that resizing makes while you append n elements one at a time.

If capacity **doubles** each time, starting from capacity 1, the resizes copy 1, then 2, then 4, and so on, each resize copying the whole old array. Every resize copies one more element than all the earlier resizes put together, so the grand total stays just under the final capacity:

```formula reference
copies = 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + C / 2
copies = C − 1
copies < 2n
where
copies: the total number of element copies made by all the resizes together
C: the final capacity, the smallest power of two that is at least n
n: the positive number of elements appended, at least one
In words: each resize copies as many elements as all the earlier resizes put together, plus one, so the grand total is always just under the final capacity, which is less than twice the number of elements.
```

For example, 17 appends end at capacity 32 after 31 copies, fewer than two per append. Spread over n appends, that is fewer than two copies per append: **amortised O(1)**. *Amortised* means averaged over a long run of operations: an occasional append is expensive, but the total for n appends is still proportional to n.

### Any constant factor works; the factor sets the trade-off

Growing by any constant factor greater than 1 works. Going backwards from the last resize, each earlier resize copied a fixed fraction as many elements as the one after it, so the copies form a shrinking **geometric series** whose total is a constant multiple of the final capacity.

```formula reference
copies ≈ C / (r − 1)
where
copies: the total number of element copies made by all the resizes together
C: the final capacity
r: the growth factor: each resize multiplies the capacity by r, which must be greater than 1 (2 means doubling, 1.5 means grow by half)
≈: approximately equal to; integer rounding and the small starting capacity are ignored
In words: total copying is a fixed multiple of the final capacity. The closer the growth factor is to 1, the larger that multiple: doubling copies about one element per final slot, growing by half copies about two.
```

The copy counts in the table describe the moment the array has just filled its final capacity. Just after a resize, the capacity can instead approach the growth factor times the live length, so the copies per live item are higher; that is also when the most capacity sits empty, as the last column shows.

| Growth factor | Copies per final item | Most capacity left empty |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | about one | about a half |
| 1.5 | about two | about a third |
| 1.125 | about eight | about a ninth |

Every factor gives a total proportional to n, so append stays amortised O(1). The choice is a trade-off: a smaller factor wastes less memory just after growing but pays a larger copying constant.

### Fixed increments fail

Growing by a constant *amount* (say +10 slots) does not work. A resize now happens every ten appends, and each one copies everything stored so far, so the copies form an **arithmetic series** that grows with the square of n:

```formula reference
copies ≈ n^2 / (2c)
where
copies: the total number of element copies made by all the resizes together
n: the positive number of elements appended, at least one
c: the fixed number of slots added at each resize, e.g. 10
≈: approximately equal to; small end effects are ignored
In words: adding a fixed number of slots means a resize every few appends, and each one copies everything so far, so total copying grows with the square of the number of appends. A bigger fixed step only divides that total by a constant.
```

With ten-slot increments and a million appends, that is about fifty billion copies, against about a million for doubling. That is O(n²), **quadratic** time.

> [!warning] Amortised is not worst case
> An individual append that triggers a resize is O(n). If you append to a 10-million-element vector in a latency-sensitive loop, that one append copies 10 million elements. When you know the final size, reserve it up front.

## Key takeaways
- Multiply capacity by a constant factor greater than one to bound total copying.
- A smaller factor trades extra copying for less empty capacity; a fixed increment makes total copying quadratic.

## Further reading
- [Dynamic array — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_array)

questions.prompt: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and **doubles** whenever an append finds it full. You append 17 elements to an empty array. Which statement best describes the copying done by resizing?

options.text: The last resize alone copies 16 elements, so the total copying is quadratic in the number of appends
options.explanation: The last resize is the biggest, but the earlier ones shrink by half each time going backwards. Their sum stays below twice the append count, which is linear, not quadratic.

options.text: Every append copies about half the array on average, so append is O(n)
options.explanation: Only the five appends that trigger a resize copy anything; the other twelve write into spare capacity. Averaged over the run, copying is under two elements per append.

options.text: Each resize copies one more element than all earlier resizes combined, so the total stays under twice the number of appends
options.explanation: Correct. The resizes copy 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 elements. Each is one more than everything before it, so the total is one less than the final capacity of 32, under twice the 17 appends. That is why append is amortised O(1).

options.text: No elements are copied, because doubling reserves room for all future appends
options.explanation: Doubling only reserves room for about as many again. Each time the array fills, the whole old block must be copied into a new one.

questions.workedExample:
Track which appends find the array full:

```
append  cap before  resize? copies
  1        1         no      0
  2        1       ->2       1
  3        2       ->4       2
  4        4         no      0
  5        4       ->8       4
  9        8       ->16      8
 17       16       ->32     16
```

1. Only five of the seventeen appends resize, and the gaps between resizes double each time.
2. Each resize copies the whole old array, so the copy sizes double too: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
3. In a doubling sequence, each term is one more than the sum of all the terms before it. So the last resize (16) is bigger than all the others combined (15), and the total is under twice the last one.
4. The last resize copied fewer elements than were appended, so total copying is under twice the append count: fewer than two copies per append on average.
5. That is the amortised argument: the occasional expensive append is paid for by the many cheap ones, so append is amortised O(1) even though a single resizing append is O(n).

questions.prompt: Starting empty with capacity 100, a home-grown dynamic array grows by a fixed **100 slots** each time it fills. A job appends 1,000,000 items. Roughly how does the total copying work scale?

options.text: O(n): about one copy per append
options.explanation: That holds for geometric growth. With fixed increments, each resize copies a larger array, and there is one every 100 appends.

options.text: O(n log n)
options.explanation: There's no halving or doubling here, so no log factor appears. The copies form an arithmetic series.

options.text: O(1), because each resize only adds 100 slots
options.explanation: Adding the slots is cheap, but the resize must copy every existing element into the new block. That copy is the expensive part.

options.text: O(n²): every resize copies everything stored so far, and a resize comes every 100 appends
options.explanation: Correct. Each resize copies a hundred more elements than the one before, and there is one every hundred appends. That arithmetic series grows with the square of the append count: billions of copies for a million appends.

questions.workedExample:
Here n is the number of items appended (one million) and the fixed growth step is 100 slots.

1. A resize happens every hundred appends, so there are about ten thousand resizes, a number that itself grows with n.
2. Each resize copies every element stored so far: one hundred, then two hundred, then three hundred, and so on up to nearly a million.
3. Those copy sizes grow by a fixed amount each time, so their sum is an arithmetic series: roughly the number of resizes times the average copy size, about half a million. Both factors grow with n, so the total grows with n²: about five billion copies here.
4. Compare doubling: total copying stays under twice the number of appends, under two million copies for the same job.
5. A bigger fixed step (say 10,000 slots) divides the total by a constant but leaves it quadratic. The fix is to multiply capacity (by 1.5 or 2), not add to it.

Option B, O(n log n), would need a factor of log n, the number of times n can be halved before reaching 1. Nothing halves or doubles here, so no log factor appears.

questions.prompt: A team changes its dynamic array's growth factor from **2** to **1.5** to save memory. Over a long run of appends, what should they expect?

options.text: Append becomes O(n log n) in total, because smaller steps mean more resizes
options.explanation: There are more resizes, but the copy sizes still shrink geometrically going backwards from the last one. Their sum is a constant multiple of the final capacity, so no log factor appears.

options.text: Total copying stays linear but its constant rises, roughly from one copy per final item to two, while the worst empty fraction after growth falls from about half to about a third
options.explanation: Correct. Any factor greater than 1 keeps append amortised O(1). Closer to 1 means more frequent, smaller resizes, so more total copying, but less capacity left empty just after a resize.

options.text: Total copying falls, because each resize copies a smaller array
options.explanation: Each resize is smaller, but resizes come more often. The total copying goes up, not down.

options.text: Append loses its amortised O(1) guarantee, because only doubling gives that
options.explanation: Any constant factor greater than 1 gives amortised O(1) appends. CPython lists grow by only about an eighth and still have amortised O(1) append.

questions.workedExample:
Here n is the number of elements appended.

1. With a growth factor, each earlier resize copied a fixed fraction of the one after it, so all the copies add up to a constant multiple of the final capacity. That keeps total copying linear and append amortised O(1) for any factor greater than 1.
2. The multiple depends on how close the factor is to 1. At a full-capacity endpoint, doubling copies about one element per final item; growing by half copies about two; growing by an eighth copies about eight.
3. The benefit is memory. Just after a resize, a doubled array can be almost half empty, while one grown by half is at most about a third empty.
4. So the team trades a larger copying constant for less wasted capacity. Neither choice changes the complexity class; a fixed *additive* step would.
5. A single resizing append is still O(n) in both cases. If latency spikes matter, reserve the final size in advance.

lessons.title: Array layouts in Python, Java and C++
lessons.summary: Python lists and Java generic lists store references; vector stores values directly.
lessons.body:
The previous units established contiguous slots and amortised growth. The slot may contain a raw value or a reference to a separate object: the language runtime decides. Details below refer to CPython and OpenJDK 21 where named, rather than every implementation of Python or Java.

## Real implementations

### Python `list`

A Python list is a dynamic array of **pointers** to objects (8 bytes each on a conventional 64-bit CPython build), not of the values themselves. `[1, 2, 3]` stores three pointers to three separate `int` objects elsewhere on the heap.

CPython over-allocates by about **12.5%** plus a small constant. When a list needs room for more elements, `list_resize` in the CPython source picks the new capacity like this:

```formula reference
new ≈ n + n / 8 + 6
where
new: the new capacity (number of pointer slots) CPython allocates
n: the number of elements the list must now hold
≈: approximately: in the real code n/8 is rounded down to a whole number and the result is rounded down to a multiple of 4
In words: CPython makes room for the elements needed, plus about an eighth more, plus a few spare slots so small lists don't resize on every append. That is a growth factor of only about 1.125, much milder than doubling.
```

The source comments give the capacity sequence for one-at-a-time appends as 0, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76... Two details are worth knowing, both specific to the CPython version you run (checked here against the 3.14 source):

- A large bulk extension, where the requested growth is bigger than the proposed spare room, gets almost no spare capacity.
- A conventional GIL-enabled build resizes with `realloc`, which can sometimes extend the block in place; the free-threaded build allocates new storage and copies the references across.

The mild factor saves memory while still giving amortised O(1) append, as the previous unit showed for any factor above 1. `sys.getsizeof` on a list reveals backing-capacity jumps for your particular build.

For a list of n elements:

- `append` and `pop()` are amortised O(1).
- `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` are O(n). Use `collections.deque` for a queue (covered later in this module).
- For dense numbers, `array.array` or NumPy store raw values contiguously, which is far more compact and cache-friendly.

### Java `ArrayList`

`ArrayList` wraps an `Object[]`. A default-constructed list allocates its 10-slot backing array lazily, on the first `add`. When it fills, OpenJDK 21 grows it by about **1.5x**: the source asks for the old capacity plus half of it, rounded down (written `old + (old >> 1)`, where `>> 1` shifts the bits right one place). From 10 slots that gives 15, then 22, then 33. A larger required minimum or the array-size limit can override that. `ensureCapacity(n)` or `new ArrayList<>(n)` pre-sizes it to hold n elements.

Because Java generics only hold objects, `ArrayList<Integer>` stores references to boxed `Integer` objects. An `int[]` of a million elements is about 4 MB; an `ArrayList<Integer>` of a million is several times that (the exact figure depends on the JVM's object layout), plus the pointer chasing.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: An address book versus a row of houses
> An address book has equal-sized lines, each holding the address of a house somewhere in town. A terrace of identical houses, by contrast, *is* the row of homes.
>
> **How it maps:** A Python `list` or Java `ArrayList<Integer>` is the address book: its contiguous slots hold references, and each value lives in its own object elsewhere on the heap. A C++ `vector<int>`, Java `int[]` or NumPy array is the terrace: the values themselves sit side by side. Reading every value from the address book means a trip to each house, which is the extra indirection and cache cost.
>
> **Where it stops:** Several address-book lines can name the same house, just as several list slots can reference one object, and the reference model is what lets a Python list hold mixed types. Real memory cost also includes object headers and allocator overhead that the picture leaves out.

### C++ `std::vector`

`vector` stores elements directly and contiguously. The standard requires amortised constant `push_back` but leaves the growth factor to the implementation: current library sources show libstdc++ and libc++ doubling the capacity and MSVC's library growing it by half for ordinary one-at-a-time growth, but those are implementation details rather than portable guarantees.

`reserve(n)` ensures capacity is at least n without changing size; it does not shrink existing capacity. The crucial pitfall is **iterator invalidation**: a reallocation moves every element, so any pointer, reference or iterator into the vector becomes dangling.

```cpp
std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3};
int& first = v[0];
v.push_back(4);  // may reallocate
// 'first' may now dangle: using it is
// undefined behaviour
```

## Key takeaways
- Python lists and Java generic lists store references; vector stores values directly.
- Reserve space before keeping C++ pointers into a vector.

lessons.title: Shrinking without resize thrashing
lessons.summary: Leave a gap between growth and shrink thresholds.
lessons.body:
Growing a dynamic array pays for occasional copying by leaving spare room for later operations. Shrinking must also leave room between resize boundaries; otherwise a push and pop can undo each other’s expensive allocation. Here n denotes the current number of live elements.

## Shrinking and other pitfalls

- **Shrink thrash.** If you double when full and halve as soon as a pop leaves the array half full or less, a workload that alternates push and pop right at the boundary resizes on every operation. The standard fix is to halve only when the array falls to a **quarter** full, so many cheap operations must happen between any two resizes. CPython's lists reallocate to shrink only when the length drops below half the allocated size, and then keep some room to spare. From CPython 3.14.9 and 3.15.1 (October 2026), a list with 32 or fewer allocated slots is no longer shrunk at all; details like this vary by version.
- **Wasted capacity.** After growth, up to half the slots (with doubling) may be empty. C++ shrink_to_fit makes a nonbinding request to reduce capacity; Java trimToSize reduces backing capacity to size. Allocators and garbage collectors determine when memory is reclaimed or returned to the OS.
- **Off-by-one errors.** The last valid index is one less than the array length. In C there is no bounds check, so reading or writing `a[len]` has undefined behavior, which can corrupt memory, crash or behave unpredictably, a classic source of security bugs.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A thermostat with a dead band
> A heating thermostat that switches on below 20 °C and off above 20 °C would click on and off every few seconds as the room hovers around 20 °C. Real thermostats leave a gap, say on at 19.5 °C and off at 20.5 °C, so each switch is followed by a calm stretch.
>
> **How it maps:** Growing when full and shrinking when half full puts the two switching points at the same length after a resize, so alternating push and pop toggles the expensive resize every time. Shrinking only at a quarter full is the dead band: after any resize, many cheap operations must happen before the next one.
>
> **Where it stops:** Switching a boiler costs about the same each time, whereas each resize copies every live element, so its cost grows with the array. The array's thresholds are exact element counts, not noisy temperature readings.

## Key takeaways
- Leave a gap between growth and shrink thresholds.
- Capacity reclamation and bounds safety are separate from append amortisation.

## Further reading
- [Dynamic array — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_array)
- [CPython listobject.c (list_resize)](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Objects/listobject.c)
- [std::vector — cppreference](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector)
- [ArrayList — Java SE 21 API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/ArrayList.html)

options.explanation: The amortised guarantee breaks here: the policy lets a single cheap operation undo the resize just paid for.

```
op    len   cap   resize
push  1025  2048  grow, copy 1024
pop   1024  1024  shrink, copy 1024
push  1025  2048  grow, copy 1024
pop   1024  1024  shrink, copy 1024
```

Every single operation copies about 1,000 elements, so the 'amortised O(1)' stack is now O(n) per operation, where n is the number of elements (about 1,024).

Fix: **shrink to half only when length falls to a quarter of capacity**. After growing to 2,048, you'd need to pop down to 512 before shrinking, so at least about n/2 cheap operations separate any two resizes. That restores amortised O(1). (Even a strict 'below half' rule is fragile: a push, pop, pop, push, push pattern still thrashes.)

lessons.title: Immutable strings and sharing
lessons.summary: Rebinding a variable leaves other aliases pointing at the old string.
lessons.body:
A string represents a sequence of text units. Many implementations store those units in an array, but strings come with two complications that trip up beginners and experienced engineers alike:

1. In most modern languages they are **immutable**: you can never change one, only make a new one.
2. A "character" is not as simple as it sounds. How many bytes it takes depends on the **character encoding**.

Both have real performance and correctness consequences.

## Immutability

In Python, Java, JavaScript, C# and Go, a string object can never be modified after it is created.

```python
s = "hello"
s[0] = "H"      # TypeError: 'str' object
                # does not support item
                # assignment
s = "H" + s[1:] # builds a new string
```

Operations that look like modification (`upper()`, `replace()`, `+`) return an immutable string value and leave the original contents alone; an implementation may reuse an existing object when the result is unchanged. A variable can be re-pointed at a new string, but any other variable still pointing at the old one sees no change.

```python
s = "hello"
t = s
s += " world"
print(t)        # hello
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Bookmarks in printed editions
> Two readers keep bookmarks in the same printed edition of a guidebook. When the publisher corrects it, they print a new edition; nobody rewrites the old pages. A reader who switches to the new edition sees the change, and the other reader's bookmark still sits in the old edition.
>
> **How it maps:** The printed edition is the string object, and each bookmark is a variable holding a reference. `s += " world"` prints a new edition and moves only `s`'s bookmark, so `t` still reads `"hello"`.
>
> **Where it stops:** A runtime may hand several readers the very same copy through interning, and CPython can sometimes extend a string in place when no other reference exists, because nobody could observe the difference. Unlike a print run, making a new string costs time proportional to its length.

C++ std::string and Rust String are mutable growable buffers with separate borrowed-view types, std::string_view and &str. C char arrays can be mutable but C does not provide those ownership/view types.

### Why make strings immutable?

- **Safe as hash keys.** A dict or HashMap stores a key in a bucket chosen by its hash. If the key could change, it would sit in the wrong bucket forever. Immutable strings can also **cache** their hash: Python and Java compute it once and store it.
- **Free sharing.** Many variables, threads or data structures can point at the same string with no copying and no locks, because nobody can change it.
- **Interning.** Identical literals can share one object. Java interns string literals; CPython interns many identifiers and short strings.
- **Security.** A checked string value cannot change through an alias. This does not prevent the file, permissions or other external resource named by it from changing between check and use.

Changing the text generally requires producing another value; allocation and copying may be optimized when observable immutability is preserved.

## Key takeaways
- Rebinding a variable leaves other aliases pointing at the old string.
- Immutability enables stable hash keys; external resources can still change.

## Further reading
- [Python built-in types: text sequences](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html)
- [String interning — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_interning)

4. `t` was never touched, so it still sees "data".

options.text: Strings are shorter than lists
options.explanation: Length has nothing to do with it; a 1 MB string is a valid key, an empty list is not.

options.text: Strings are immutable, so their hash can never change after the key is stored
options.explanation: Correct. A dict places each key in a slot chosen by its hash. A mutable key could change, its hash would no longer match its slot, and lookups would fail. Strings can even cache their hash.

options.text: Lists are stored as linked lists, which can't be hashed
options.explanation: Python lists are dynamic arrays, and anything can in principle be hashed. The issue is that a list's contents, and so its hash, could change while it's a key.

options.explanation: Any hashable object works, including tuples of hashable elements and appropriate custom objects. Some mutable objects hash by their identity, which never changes; lists deliberately lack a hash compatible with their content equality.

1. `d["apple"] = 1` computes `hash("apple")` and stores the entry in the slot that hash points to.
2. Later, `d["apple"]` hashes again and looks in the same slot. This works only if the hash is stable.
3. If keys could mutate, `k.append(4)` would change `hash(k)`, but the entry would still sit in the old slot: lost.
4. Python prevents this by making lists unhashable. A tuple works as a sequence key only when all its elements are hashable.
5. Bonus: since a str can't change, CPython computes its hash once and caches it in the object.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of making strings immutable, as Java and Python do? Select all that apply.

options.text: A string's hash code can be computed once and cached, making repeated map lookups cheaper
options.explanation: Correct. Java's `String.hashCode()` and CPython's str hash are cached on the object because the contents can never change.

options.text: Strings can be shared between threads without locks
options.explanation: Correct. No thread can modify a shared string, so there are no data races on its contents.

options.text: Concatenation in a loop becomes O(n)
options.explanation: Incorrect. Immutability is exactly why naive concatenation of n pieces is O(n²): a flat-buffer implementation without in-place optimization recopies the growing prefix.

options.text: Identical strings can be interned so that many references share one object
options.explanation: Correct. Interning is only safe because nobody can change the shared string out from under the other users.

options.text: It allows O(1) indexing in UTF-8
options.explanation: Incorrect. Immutability says nothing about encoding. O(1) indexing comes from fixed-width storage (Latin-1, UTF-16 units, PEP 393), not from immutability; UTF-8 indexing by code point is O(n) either way.

questions.workedExample:
Think about what each benefit requires:

1. **Hash caching** requires that the contents never change after the first `hashCode()` call. Immutability guarantees that.
2. **Lock-free sharing** requires no writers. Immutability means there are none.
3. **Interning** requires that changing one 'copy' can't affect another. With immutability there's no changing.
4. **Concatenation** is the price you pay: edits generally produce new values, with allocation depending on implementation. Use builders.
5. **Indexing speed** is a storage-layout question. A mutable UTF-8 string of n bytes would still need an O(n) scan to find code point i.

lessons.title: Bytes, code points and grapheme clusters
lessons.summary: Byte length, code-unit length and visible-character length can differ.
lessons.body:
A string represents text, but byte storage and visible characters are different layers. This unit follows text from its stored bytes through runtime indexing to grapheme clusters, so you can choose the length limit your application actually needs.

## Encoding basics

Computers store bytes, not letters. A **character encoding** maps characters to bytes.

- **ASCII** covers 128 characters (English letters, digits, punctuation) in 7 bits.
- **Unicode** assigns a number, a **code point**, to over 150,000 characters: `U+0041` is `A`, `U+00E9` is `é`, `U+1F600` is 😀.
- **UTF-8** stores each Unicode scalar value in 1 to 4 bytes; surrogate code points are excluded. ASCII characters take 1 byte, so plain ASCII text is valid UTF-8. It is the dominant encoding on the web and in files.
- **UTF-16** uses 2 bytes for most common characters and 4 bytes (a **surrogate pair**) for the rest, including most emoji.

```
char   code point  UTF-8 bytes  UTF-16 units
A      U+0041      1            1
é      U+00E9      2            1
€      U+20AC      3            1
😀     U+1F600     4            2
```

### What does "length" mean?

Different languages count different things:

```python
s = "café"
len(s)                  # 4 code points
len(s.encode("utf-8"))  # 5 bytes
len("😀")               # 1
```

In Java and JavaScript, `"😀".length()` / `"😀".length` is **2**, because they count UTF-16 code units. Slicing such a string in the wrong place splits a surrogate pair and produces garbage.

Even code points aren't what a reader thinks of as a character. `é` can be one code point (`U+00E9`) or two (`e` plus a combining accent `U+0301`). The two forms look identical but compare unequal unless you apply **Unicode normalisation** to both (Python's `unicodedata.normalize`). A flag emoji like 🇬🇧 is two code points. What users perceive as one character is a **grapheme cluster**.

### How runtimes store strings

- **CPython** (PEP 393) picks 1, 2 or 4 bytes per code point for each string, based on the widest character it contains. Every code point then has a fixed width, so `s[i]` stays O(1). One emoji in a long ASCII string makes the whole string 4 bytes per character.
- **Java** 9+ uses "compact strings": Latin-1 (1 byte per char) when possible, otherwise UTF-16.
- **Rust** `String` stores valid UTF-8. **Go strings** are arbitrary byte sequences, conventionally UTF-8 for text. Getting the *i*-th code point of an n-byte string means scanning from the start, O(n), which is why Rust doesn't let you write `s[i]` on a `String` and Go's `s[i]` gives you a byte.

## Key takeaways
- Byte length, code-unit length and visible-character length can differ.
- Runtime representation determines what an index means and costs.

## Further reading
- [PEP 393 — Flexible String Representation](https://peps.python.org/pep-0393/)
- [UTF-8 — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8)
- [The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Must Know About Unicode — Joel Spolsky](https://www.joelonsoftware.com/2003/10/08/the-absolute-minimum-every-software-developer-absolutely-positively-must-know-about-unicode-and-character-sets-no-excuses/)
- [Python built-in types: text sequences](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html)

3. Bytes: 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = **5**.

Caveat: if the é were typed as `e` + combining accent U+0301, `len(s)` would be 5 and the UTF-8 length 6, even though it looks identical. That's why you normalise text before comparing or counting it.

lessons.title: Building strings without repeated copying
lessons.summary: Repeated full-copy concatenation sums growing prefixes.
lessons.body:
An immutable string cannot be observably changed through an alias. A full-copy concatenation creates the combined value; repeat that operation and you repeatedly copy earlier prefixes. The cost model below explicitly excludes optimisations that extend an unshared buffer in place.

## Concatenation cost

In the full-copy model, joining two immutable strings creates a new value with space for both inputs and copies every code unit of each. So `"abc" + "de"` copies 5 characters, and appending one character to a 1,000-character string copies 1,001. One concatenation costs time in proportion to the combined length. Observable immutability does not forbid optimising an unshared internal buffer, which is why the CPython caveat below matters.

Now put it in a loop:

```python
result = ""
for word in words:   # n words
    result += word   # full-copy model
```

Each pass copies everything built so far plus the new word, so each pass costs more than the last. Adding up passes whose cost grows by a fixed amount gives an arithmetic series:

```formula reference
total ≈ kn^2 / 2
where
total: the number of characters copied over the whole loop
n: the number of words joined
k: the length of each word, in characters (assumed all equal)
≈: approximately equal to; small end effects are ignored for large n
In words: pass i copies about i words' worth of characters, so the total grows with the square of the number of words: doubling the word count roughly quadruples the copying.
```

That's quadratic: **O(n²)** for a fixed word length. For 100,000 one-character pieces, that is about five billion character copies, where a single join would copy 100,000.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Recopying a manuscript
> Imagine keeping a story only as one handwritten fair copy. To add a sentence, you write out a fresh copy of the whole story plus the new sentence. Early on that is quick; by the hundredth sentence, each addition means rewriting a hundred sentences. Keeping the sentences on separate cards and copying them out once at the end avoids all that rewriting.
>
> **How it maps:** The fair copy is the immutable string, each fresh copy is a full-copy concatenation, and the stack of cards is the list of parts that `"".join` copies exactly once.
>
> **Where it stops:** A runtime that knows nobody else holds the string may quietly extend it in place, which is like being allowed to append to the last page. Copying memory is also far faster than handwriting, so the problem only shows up for large n.

> [!note] CPython sometimes cheats
> CPython can extend `result` in place when nothing else references it, which often makes this loop fast in practice. It's an implementation detail: it disappears if another reference exists, and PEP 8 says not to rely on it. It is not a portable guarantee across Python implementations.

### The fix: collect, then join

Gather the pieces in a list (amortised O(1) appends), then join once. `join` measures the combined length of the pieces, allocates once, and copies each piece once: **O(number of pieces + output length)**.

```python
parts = []
for word in words:
    # Collect pieces without copying
    # prefixes.
    parts.append(word)
# Build the complete text in one pass.
result = "".join(parts)
```

In Java, use `StringBuilder`, a mutable, growable character buffer (a dynamic array, so appending k units costs amortised O(k + 1)):

```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String w : words) {
    // Append into the growable builder.
    sb.append(w);
}
// Produce the final immutable text value.
String result = sb.toString();
```

> [!warning] The compiler won't save you in a loop
> `javac` turns a single expression like `a + b + c` into one efficient concatenation. But `s = s + w` inside a loop still creates growing immutable results. For n equal-sized pieces and no cross-iteration optimisation, the loop remains O(n²).

## Key takeaways
- Repeated full-copy concatenation sums growing prefixes.
- Collect pieces and join once, or use a mutable builder.

## Further reading
- [StringBuilder — Java SE 21 API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/StringBuilder.html)
- [Python built-in types: text sequences](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html)
- [PEP 8 — string-concatenation portability](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/)

lessons.title: String operations, slices and text pitfalls
lessons.summary: Repeated slices can make an otherwise linear recursion quadratic.
lessons.body:
For these bounds, n is the string length in the units the runtime indexes, and basic element comparisons have constant cost. The earlier encoding unit explains why these units are not necessarily bytes or visible characters. Runtime shortcuts can avoid copying a whole unchanged string; bounds here describe general proper slices and changed results.

## Common operations and their complexity

For a string `s` of length n (Python and Java, which store their length and support O(1) indexing). In the table, `a` and `b` in `s[a:b]` are the start and end positions of the slice, and m is the length of the string `t` being searched for:

| Operation | Cost | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `len(s)` | O(1) | Length is stored |
| `s[i]` | O(1) | Fixed-width units |
| `s[a:b]` | O(b − a + 1) | Proper nonempty slices copy; unchanged whole slices may reuse |
| `a == b` | O(n) | Stops at first difference |
| `t in s` | O(n·m) worst | Usually much faster |
| `upper` | O(n + 1) | Unicode case conversion; output may expand |
| literal `split`, `replace` | Depends on search and output size | Replacement can expand the output |
| `"".join(parts)` | O(pieces + output length) | Must inspect empty pieces too |

A few details matter here:

- **C's `strlen` is O(n).** C strings are byte arrays ending in a zero byte, and the length is found by scanning for it. Writing `for (i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++)` makes the loop O(n²) unless the compiler hoists the call.
- **Slices copy.** An ordinary nonempty proper CPython slice such as `s[1:]` generally copies its selected characters; empty and full unchanged slices can reuse objects. Recursive functions that pass `s[1:]` down at each level copy O(n) per call: O(n²) total. Pass indices instead. Java's `substring` has also copied since Java 7u6; earlier versions shared the parent's array, which caused memory leaks when a tiny substring kept a huge string alive.
- **Substring search.** A naive search tries every start position, O(n·m) in the worst case. Library implementations use cleverer algorithms and are fast on typical text; CPython adopted the linear-time two-way algorithm for longer needles in Python 3.10. Linear-time algorithms such as KMP appear in a later module.
- **Hashing** is O(n) the first time, but Python and Java cache the result on the string object.

## Pitfalls in practice

- **Byte limits vs character limits.** A database column, HTTP header or SMS segment limited in bytes can overflow on text that looks short. Truncating UTF-8 at a byte boundary can slice a character in half and produce invalid data. Truncate on code points (or graphemes), then check the byte length.
- **Identity vs equality.** In Python, `a is b` asks "same object?", not "same text?". Interning makes it accidentally true for some literals and false for strings built at runtime. In Java, `==` on `String` compares references; use `.equals()`.
- **Repeated `replace` or `+` in hot paths.** Each creates a new string. Build once with a builder or `join`.
- **Reversing user-visible text.** `s[::-1]` reverses code points, which mangles combining accents and multi-code-point emoji.

## Key takeaways
- Repeated slices can make an otherwise linear recursion quadratic.
- Use text equality and preserve encoding or grapheme boundaries.

## Further reading
- [Python built-in types: text sequences](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html)

options.explanation: Correct. Each slice is 2 characters shorter than the last, so about n/2 calls each copy about n/2 characters on average: quadratic total copying. Passing indices `lo, hi` instead makes it O(n).

options.text: O(n): a linear number of calls, each doing O(1) comparisons
options.explanation: The comparison is O(1), but `s[1:-1]` is not: slicing a Python str copies the characters into a new string.

options.text: O(2ⁿ), because it's recursive

questions.workedExample:
1. Each recursive call removes one code point from each end, so a palindrome of length n makes about n/2 calls.
2. Each call builds `s[1:-1]`: a new str two characters shorter than its input. Copying cost is proportional to that length.
3. The slice lengths run n − 2, n − 4, ... down to 0 or 1: about n/2 slices averaging about n/2 characters, so roughly a quarter of n² characters copied in total. That is O(n²), about 250,000 copies for a 1,000-character palindrome.

```python
    lo, hi = 0, len(s) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        if s[lo] != s[hi]:
            return False
        # Move inward without
        # allocating a slice.
        lo += 1
        # Compare the next symmetric
        # position.
        hi -= 1
    return True
```

An O(log n) recursion would need the string to halve on every call. Here it shrinks by only 2.

options.text: O(n log n)

questions.prompt: Before Java 7u6, `String.substring` returned a view sharing the parent's `char[]`. A service read 50-million-byte ASCII log files into Strings, kept a 20-character `substring` of each as an ID in a long-lived cache, and discarded the rest. What happened?

options.text: Each cached ID kept its file's whole backing array (about 100 MB) alive, causing a memory leak
options.explanation: Correct. The GC can't free the parent array while any substring still references it. This is why Java 7u6 changed `substring` to copy: O(k) time for a k-character substring, but no hidden retention.

options.text: Memory use stayed small, since each ID was only 20 characters
options.explanation: That's the post-7u6 behaviour, where substring copies. With sharing, each tiny ID kept a reference to the entire 50-million-character array.

options.text: The IDs became corrupted when the original Strings were garbage-collected
options.explanation: The GC never frees memory that's still reachable. The shared array stayed alive precisely because the substrings referenced it, so nothing was corrupted.

options.text: `substring` threw an exception for strings over 2 GB
options.explanation: The files were 50 MB each, well within array limits. The problem was retention, not size.

questions.workedExample:
1. Old design: `String` held `(char[] value, int offset, int count)`. `substring` made a new String with the same `value` and a different offset/count: O(1) time, no copying.
2. Downside: the 20-character ID still references the 50-million-char backing array (about 100 MB, since Java chars were 2 bytes).
3. 1,000 cached IDs → up to ~100 GB of arrays that can't be collected.
4. Workaround then: `new String(s.substring(a, b))` forced a copy.
5. Since 7u6, `substring` copies the k characters. Ordinary proper CPython str slices copy; empty or whole-string slices can reuse existing objects. The trade-off: sharing makes slicing O(1) but risks retention; copying a k-character slice makes it O(k) but predictable.

lessons.title: Nodes, traversal and positional search
lessons.summary: A node stores a value and a link rather than a positional address shortcut.
lessons.body:
An array keeps its elements side by side. A **linked list** gives that up: each element lives in its own **node**, anywhere in memory, and each node holds a pointer to the next one.

```
head
 |
 v
[3|*]--->[8|*]--->[5|*]--->None
 val next
```

That one change flips the trade-offs. For a list of n elements:

- You can no longer jump to element `i`; you must walk there. Access becomes **O(n)**.
- But if you already hold a node, you can insert or remove next to it by rewiring a couple of pointers, with no shifting. That's **O(1)**.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A treasure hunt
> In a treasure hunt each clue tells you where the next clue is hidden. To reach clue 5 you must find clues 1 to 4 first, but slipping a new clue in after clue 3 only means rewriting clue 3 to point at it.
>
> **How it maps:** Each clue is a node, the directions on it are the `next` pointer, and the first clue's location is `head`. Following clues one by one is traversal, so reaching position k costs k hops, while inserting after a clue you are holding is a constant-time rewire.
>
> **Where it stops:** Following a pointer takes nanoseconds, not a walk across a park, although each hop can still miss the cache. A real list also needs a definite end, where the last node's `next` is `None`, and unlike paper clues, nodes are never consumed by reading them.

Linked lists are a staple of interviews and textbooks. In production code they are less common than you might expect, and knowing *why* is part of mastering them.

## Singly linked lists

Each node has a value and a `next` pointer. The list itself is just a reference to the first node, the **head node** (or just the head). The last node's `next` is `None`.

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

# build 3 -> 8 -> 5
head = Node(3, Node(8, Node(5)))
```

### Traversal and search

```python
def find(head, target):
    cur = head
    while cur:
        if cur.val == target:
            return cur
        # Follow the link, not a numeric
        # index.
        cur = cur.next
    return None
```

Getting the k-th element means following k pointers, so it costs O(k + 1), including the final value read; this is O(n) in the worst case for a list of n nodes. Searching for a value is O(n) too: you may have to look at every node.

### Avoid repeating positional traversal

Calling an indexed accessor repeatedly does not retain the previous traversal position. A Java LinkedList lookup starts from whichever end is nearer the requested position. That is helpful for one lookup but still repeats walking when an index-based loop visits every element.

For one hundred thousand nodes, an index loop that calls `get(i)` for every position re-walks from an end each time, adding up to billions of dependent pointer hops: quadratic total work. An iterator instead remembers the current node and follows one link per next element, giving a single linear traversal. When you need repeated arbitrary positional lookup, a dynamic array usually matches the access pattern better.

This explains an important distinction: a linked list can support a constant-time update next to a handle you already hold, but locating that handle is a different operation. The next unit examines those updates, including the order in which successor links must change.

## Key takeaways
- A node stores a value and a link rather than a positional address shortcut.
- Repeated indexed access to a linked list can repeat the traversal.

## Further reading
- [Linked list — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linked_list)
- [LinkedList — Java SE 21 API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/LinkedList.html)

2. `cur = cur.next` takes you to node 1, then node 2, and so on.

questions.workedExample:
Here n is the number of orders, 100,000.

1. `LinkedList.get(i)` starts from the head if `i` is in the first half, otherwise from the tail. It does not remember where the previous call stopped.
2. Positions near the middle cost about n/2 hops each; positions near the ends cost almost nothing. On average a call walks about a quarter of the list.
3. The loop makes n calls, so the total is about a quarter of n² hops: around 2.5 billion here, each a dependent load whose cache-hit rate depends on allocation and working set. That is O(n²) for what should be one pass.
4. Fix A: `for (Order o : orders) process(o);` → the iterator keeps its current node, so one pass of n hops.
5. Fix B: use `ArrayList`, where `get(i)` is O(1).

Rule: inside a loop, iterate over a linked list instead of calling `get(i)` on it.

lessons.title: Rewiring a singly linked list
lessons.summary: Preserve the old successor before replacing a link.
lessons.body:
A singly linked node has a value and a next reference. Use the Node class from the preceding unit. The operations below assume a finite, acyclic list and valid node handles; deletion also needs a successor to remove. Here n is the number of nodes.

### Insertion

Inserting at the head is O(1), and so is inserting after a node you already hold:

```python
# push to front
head = Node(1, head)

# insert x after node p
# Keep the old suffix in the new node.
p.next = Node(x, p.next)
```

```
before:  p -> [8] -> [5]
after:   p -> [x] -> [8] -> [5]
```

Order matters. Create the new node pointing at `p.next` *first*, then point `p` at it. Do it the other way round and you lose the rest of the list.

Inserting at the tail of an n-node list is O(n), because you must walk to the last node, unless you also keep a `tail` pointer, in which case it is O(1).

### Deletion

To remove a node you need the node **before** it, so you can skip over it:

```python
# remove the node after p
# Bypass one existing successor node.
p.next = p.next.next
```

This is the singly linked list's big weakness. Given only a pointer to a non-head node, you cannot unlink that node in O(1), because you cannot reach its predecessor without walking from the head. Copying the successor’s value into it and skipping the successor is not the same operation: it changes what existing handles observe and fails at the tail. Removing the head is a special case (`head = head.next`), and that special-casing is a common source of bugs.

## Key takeaways
- Preserve the old successor before replacing a link.
- Deleting a real node requires its predecessor; copying a value is a different operation.

## Further reading
- [Linked list — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linked_list)

questions.prompt:
Using `Node(val, next)`, what does this print?

```python
    head = Node(x, head)
p = head.next
p.next = Node(9, p.next)
head = head.next
while head:
    print(head.val, end=" ")
    head = head.next
```

That's the list before the last line. `head = head.next` then drops the first node, 3.
The insert after `p` (node 2) did happen. `Node(9, p.next)` points 9 at node 1, then `p.next` points at 9.
Correct. The loop builds 3 → 2 → 1, the insert makes 3 → 2 → 9 → 1, and moving head skips the 3.

```
x=2: head -> 2 -> 1

```

Output: `2 9 1`. Note that pushing to the front reverses the input order, and that insertion after `p` creates the new node pointing at `p.next` before overwriting `p.next`.

lessons.title: Doubly linked lists and sentinels
lessons.summary: Unlinking must update both neighbours.
lessons.body:
A singly linked list has no backwards link. A doubly linked list adds a predecessor reference so both neighbours can be reconnected when a known node is removed. Constant-time claims count pointer operations on valid handles, not allocator or value-destruction time.

## Doubly linked lists

Add a `prev` pointer to every node and you can walk in both directions, and delete any node in O(1) given only that node:

```
None<-[3]<=>[8]<=>[5]->None
```

```python
def unlink(node):
    # Repair the forward neighbour link.
    node.prev.next = node.next
    # Repair the backward neighbour link.
    node.next.prev = node.prev
```

That code crashes when `node` is the head (`node.prev` is `None`) or the tail. Handling those cases with `if` statements everywhere is tedious and error-prone. Which brings us to sentinels.

## Sentinel nodes

A **sentinel** (or dummy) node is a node that holds no data and is always present. With a circular doubly linked sentinel, every real node has neighbours on both sides even when there are no other data nodes. The data sequence can be empty while the sentinel remains.

The neatest version is a **circular doubly linked list with one sentinel**: the sentinel's `next` is the first element and its `prev` is the last.

```
   +--------------------------+
   v                          |
[sent] <=> [3] <=> [8] <=> [5]
   |                          ^
   +--------------------------+

empty list: sent.next = sent.prev = sent
```

```python
class DNode:
    def __init__(self, val=None):
        self.val = val
        # An unattached node points to
        # itself.
        self.prev = self.next = self

class DList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.s = DNode()   # sentinel

    def insert_after(self, p, val):
        n = DNode(val)
        # Link the newcomer to both
        # neighbours.
        n.prev, n.next = p, p.next
        # Redirect the old successor
        # backwards.
        p.next.prev = n
        # Publish the new forward
        # connection.
        p.next = n
        return n

    def push_front(self, val):
        s = self.s
        return self.insert_after(s, val)

    def push_back(self, val):
        last = self.s.prev
        return self.insert_after(last, val)

    def remove(self, n):
        # Bypass the node when walking
        # forwards.
        n.prev.next = n.next
        # Bypass it when walking backwards.
        n.next.prev = n.prev
```

For valid handles belonging to this list, insertion and removal use a constant number of pointer updates. Do not remove the sentinel or remove a node twice. Allocation and value destruction are outside this pointer-operation model. There is no special case for an empty list, the first node or the last node. The Linux kernel's `struct list_head` uses exactly this design, with intrusive link fields embedded in containing objects.

> [!tip] The cost of a sentinel
> One extra node of memory per list. For a list with millions of entries that's nothing; for millions of tiny lists it can add up.

## Key takeaways
- Unlinking must update both neighbours.
- A circular sentinel makes every valid data-node removal use the same pointer updates.

## Further reading
- [Doubly linked list — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubly_linked_list)
- [Linux kernel API: list management](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/kernel-api.html)
- [Linux — linked-list API and circular sentinels](https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/list.html)

options.text: C, A
options.explanation: That's what forward traversal shows (A, C) reversed. But C's `prev` pointer was never updated.

options.text: C only, then an error
options.explanation: B's pointers were never cleared, so following `C.prev` reaches B and then A without error.

options.text: C, B, A
options.explanation: Correct. Forward links skip B, but `C.prev` still points to B, and `B.prev` still points to A. The list is now inconsistent in the two directions.

options.text: An infinite loop
options.explanation: No pointer was made to form a cycle. Backward links still form the original chain C → B → A → None.
