1. Before: A.next = B, B.next = C; C.prev = B, B.prev = A.
2. Buggy remove sets only `A.next = C`.
3. Forward: A → C. Looks right.
4. Backward: C.prev = **B** (unchanged) → B.prev = A → None. Output: C, B, A.
5. A doubly linked removal must patch both directions:

```python
# Repair the forward neighbour link.
node.prev.next = node.next
# Repair the backward neighbour link.
node.next.prev = node.prev
```

This kind of half-update is exactly what makes doubly linked lists error-prone, and why invariants (`x.next.prev is x` for every node) are worth asserting in tests.

questions.prompt: You implement a doubly linked list as a **circular list with a single sentinel node**. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: An empty list is a sentinel whose `next` and `prev` both point to itself
options.explanation: Correct. That's the base state, and it means `s.next` and `s.prev` are never `None`.

options.text: `remove(node)` needs no special cases for the first or last element
options.explanation: Correct. Every real node has real neighbours on both sides (possibly the sentinel), so the same two pointer updates always work.

options.text: `push_back` is O(n) because you must walk to the end
options.explanation: Incorrect. The last element is `s.prev`, available in O(1), so `push_back` is O(1).

options.text: The list is empty exactly when `s.next is s`
options.explanation: Correct. That's how the Linux kernel's `list_empty` works: the head's `next` points back at the head.

options.text: Traversal can stop when `cur is None`
options.explanation: Incorrect. Nothing is ever `None` in a circular list, so that loop never terminates. Stop when you arrive back at the sentinel.

questions.workedExample:
1. Empty: `s.next = s.prev = s`.
2. push_back(5): insert after `s.prev` (which is `s`). Now `s <-> 5 <-> s`.
3. remove(5): `5.prev.next = 5.next` → `s.next = s`; `5.next.prev = 5.prev` → `s.prev = s`. Back to empty with no `if`s.
4. Traversal:

```python
cur = s.next
while cur is not s:
    visit(cur)
    # Follow the link, not a numeric
    # index.
    cur = cur.next
```

5. For n elements, `push_back` and `remove` stay O(1) rather than O(n). The trade is one extra node of memory per list in exchange for removing every head/tail/empty branch.

lessons.title: Circular lists and production trade-offs
lessons.summary: A tail-only circular list exposes its head through the tail link.
lessons.body:
The preceding units showed why knowing the node changes a list operation’s cost. Here n is the number of data elements. Circular organisation changes termination rules; practical layout and stable-handle requirements decide whether pointer-based storage is worthwhile.

## Circular lists

In a **circular** list the last node points back to the first instead of to `None`. Circular singly linked lists are handy for round-robin scheduling: keep a pointer to the current node and advance it forever.

A neat trick: keep only a **tail pointer**. Then `tail.next` is the head, so you get O(1) access to both ends from one pointer.

The danger with circular lists is the loop condition. `while cur:` never ends; you must stop when you return to your starting node.

## Cost summary

For a sequence of n elements, keeping both head and tail handles for the doubly linked representation and using constant-time value/allocation operations:

| Operation | Array | Singly | Doubly |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access i-th | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Insert/delete at front | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |
| Insert/delete at back | O(1) amortised | See below | O(1) |
| Delete given node | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) |
| Insert after given node | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |

For a singly linked list, inserting at the back is O(1) if you keep a tail pointer, but deleting the last node is O(n), because you have to walk to its predecessor.

## The hidden costs

Big-O makes linked lists look great for insertion-heavy work. Real hardware is less kind.

- **Memory overhead.** Every node carries one or two pointers plus allocator bookkeeping. A Java `LinkedList` node is an object with three references (item, next, prev); for small elements, the overhead dwarfs the data. A Python node object costs tens of bytes before you even count the value.
- **Cache misses.** Nodes are scattered around the heap. Walking a list is a chain of dependent loads: the CPU can't fetch node 5 until node 4 tells it where node 5 is. Arrays stream through cache with prefetching.
- **Allocation.** Separately allocated nodes add allocation/reclamation work; pools and intrusive lists can avoid a per-insertion allocation.
- **Finding the spot is O(n) anyway** (for n elements). "Insert in the middle is O(1)" assumes you already hold the node. If you have to search for the position first, that search is O(n), and on an array it is a fast linear scan.

> [!example] Why locality can outweigh shifting
> A vector can beat a linked list when both first perform a linear search for the insertion point: fast contiguous scanning and shifting can outweigh the list's cheap relink, because the list's search is a chain of dependent pointer loads. No universal speed ratio applies; measure your own workload.

## When linked lists actually win

Linked lists earn their place when you **already hold a reference** to the node you want to change, or when you need properties arrays can't give:

1. **O(1) removal from the middle via a handle.** An LRU cache pairs a hash map (key to node) with a doubly linked list. On every hit it unlinks the node and moves it to the front in O(1). This is how Python's `OrderedDict` and Java's `LinkedHashMap` keep order.
2. **Stable references.** Inserting into or removing from a `std::list` never invalidates iterators to other elements. A vector's reallocation invalidates all of them.
3. **Splicing.** Relinking a run with known boundaries takes a few pointer changes, but maintaining container metadata can add work. C++ std::list range-splice between different lists is linear in the range length; whole-list and single-element splice are constant-time under their allocator preconditions.
4. **No reallocation spikes.** A linked queue never has to copy everything to grow, but allocation, reclamation and synchronization still need bounded-latency designs for hard real-time use.
5. **Intrusive lists.** In kernels and game engines, the `next`/`prev` pointers live inside the object itself, so membership needs no separate node allocation; simultaneous membership in several lists requires a separate link pair for each list.
6. **Immutable sharing.** In functional languages (Haskell, Lisp, Scala's `List`), prepending to a list creates one new node that points at the old list. Both versions remain valid and share the tail.

Many practical structures are hybrids. CPython's `collections.deque` is a doubly linked list of **blocks**, each holding 64 items. It keeps O(1) operations at both ends while getting most of an array's cache-friendliness.

## Key takeaways
- A tail-only circular list exposes its head through the tail link.
- Known handles, stable references and shared immutable tails are reasons to accept pointer overhead.

## Further reading
- [Linked list — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linked_list)
- [LinkedList — Java SE 21 API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/LinkedList.html)
- [Linux kernel API: list management](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/core-api/kernel-api.html)
- [collections.deque — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)

lessons.title: Reverse links while preserving the suffix
lessons.summary: Save the remaining suffix before flipping a next pointer.
lessons.body:
Most linked-list problems, in interviews and in real code, reduce to a few patterns. Learn these four and you can assemble the rest:

1. **Reversal**: turn every arrow around in one pass.
2. **Fast and slow pointers**: two pointers moving at different speeds.
3. **Merging**: weave two sorted lists together.
4. **Dummy heads**: a throwaway node in front so the real head is never a special case.

For a list of n nodes, the iterative patterns below use linear time, O(n), and **O(1) extra space** (a fixed handful of pointer variables, however long the list); recursive reversal is an explicit exception. Unless detecting a cycle, assume finite acyclic lists. That last part is the point: anyone can solve these problems by copying the list into an array first, but then you've spent O(n) memory.

Throughout, we use:

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next
```

## Reversal

Reversing a singly linked list in place means making every `next` point backwards. You need three pointers: the node you're working on (`cur`), the part already reversed (`prev`), and the rest of the list (`nxt`), which you must save before you break the link to it.

```python
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next   # save the rest
        cur.next = prev  # flip the arrow
        prev = cur       # grow reversed
        cur = nxt        # move on
    return prev          # new head
```

The following is an execution-state trace of the Python function on the three-node chain:

```
start   prev=None  cur=1   1->2->3
iter 1  None<-1    prev=1  cur=2
iter 2  None<-1<-2 prev=2  cur=3
iter 3  None<-1<-2<-3
        prev=3     cur=None
return 3:  3->2->1
```

Each of the n nodes is visited once: O(n) time, O(1) space.

### Recursive reversal

```python
def reverse_rec(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    # Reverse the suffix before linking
    # back.
    new_head = reverse_rec(head.next)
    head.next.next = head  # flip
    # The old head becomes the new tail.
    head.next = None
    return new_head
```

It's elegant, but on an n-node list it uses **O(n) stack space**, one frame per node. A conventional CPython build commonly starts with a recursion limit of 1,000; inspect `sys.getrecursionlimit()` rather than assuming an unchanged configuration. Under that setting a 10,000-node recursive reversal raises `RecursionError`. Prefer the loop.

## Key takeaways
- Save the remaining suffix before flipping a next pointer.
- An iterative reversal keeps a fixed pointer set; recursion retains one frame per node.

## Further reading
- [Linked list — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linked_list)
- [sys.setrecursionlimit — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html)

lessons.title: Fast and slow pointers: middle and cycles
lessons.summary: The loop condition determines which even-length middle is returned.
lessons.body:
Use the singly linked Node class from the reversal unit. In an acyclic list of n nodes, one- and two-link moves find a middle without counting the length first. On a cyclic list they instead reveal whether the same node is reached at the same time.

## Fast and slow pointers

Move one pointer (`slow`) one step at a time and another (`fast`) two steps. The gap between them grows by one each step. That simple fact answers several questions in one pass.

### Finding the middle

When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` has gone half as far.

```python
def middle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        # Two links for every one slow
        # link.
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow
```

The following execution-state trace records the Python pointer values.

```
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5
step 0: slow=1 fast=1
step 1: slow=2 fast=3
step 2: slow=3 fast=5  (stop)
middle = 3
```

For an even-length list such as `1..6`, this returns **4**, the second of the two middle nodes. If you need the first middle (useful for splitting a list in half for merge sort), use `while fast and fast.next and fast.next.next` to handle empty input too.

### Floyd's cycle detection

A bug or a malicious input can make a list loop back on itself. Walking it with `while cur:` then never ends. How do you detect a cycle?

The obvious answer is a set of visited nodes: for a list of n nodes that is O(n) time but **O(n) memory**. **Floyd's algorithm** (the "tortoise and hare") does it in O(1) memory.

If there's no cycle, `fast` falls off the end. If there is, both pointers end up circling the loop, and `fast` gains one node per step on `slow`, so it must eventually land exactly on it. It can't jump over `slow`: if `fast` is one behind, the next step brings them together.

```python
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        # Two links for every one slow
        # link.
        fast = fast.next.next
        # Compare nodes, not their stored
        # values.
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False
```

Note `is`: compare node *identity*, not values. Two different nodes can hold the same value.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Runners on a looped track
> Two runners set off along a path that leads onto a circular track. One runs twice as fast as the other. If the path is a dead end, the fast runner simply reaches the end first. If it feeds into a loop, the fast runner eventually comes round and draws level with the slow one.
>
> **How it maps:** The path is the list, the loop is a cycle, and the runners are `slow` (one link per step) and `fast` (two links per step). Drawing level is the `slow is fast` identity check; reaching the end is `fast` becoming `None`.
>
> **Where it stops:** Runners move continuously and could pass between checks, but the pointers move in whole nodes. Because `fast` gains exactly one node per step, it cannot jump over `slow` and must land on the same node.

### Bound the detection phase

Slow needs the tail length in steps to reach the cycle. Once both pointers are on it, the gap closes by one node per step, so they meet within one more lap.

```formula reference
S ≤ μ + λ
where
S: iterations until an after-movement identity check detects a meeting
μ: tail length, the link steps before the cycle entry
λ: cycle length, the number of nodes around one lap
≤: is at most
In words: detection takes at most the tail length plus one lap of the cycle, so it is linear in the number of nodes and needs only two pointers of extra memory.
```

The first meeting need not be at the entry. In the chain one, two, three, four, five with five linking back to two, the tail is one link and the cycle has four nodes. The pointers first meet at five. In an acyclic chain with three equal values, two different nodes can hold the same value without forming a cycle: identity is what matters. The next unit uses the meeting to locate the entry.

## Key takeaways
- The loop condition determines which even-length middle is returned.
- Detect a cycle by node identity, not repeated values.

## Further reading
- [Cycle detection — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_detection)
- [Linked list — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linked_list)

lessons.title: Locate the entry of a detected cycle
lessons.summary: At a meeting, the fast pointer has gained a whole number of cycle laps.
lessons.body:
First detect a meeting with the one-step slow pointer and two-step fast pointer. The preceding unit covered that identity test. This unit locates the cycle’s first node and proves why resetting one pointer works; no auxiliary set or list copying is required.

### Finding where the cycle starts

Floyd's algorithm has a second phase. After the pointers meet, put one back at the head and advance **both one step at a time**. They meet again exactly at the first node of the cycle.

```python
def cycle_start(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        # Two links for every one slow
        # link.
        fast = fast.next.next
        # Compare nodes, not their stored
        # values.
        if slow is fast:
            break
    else:
        return None        # no cycle
    # Reset only one pointer after meeting.
    p = head
    while p is not slow:
        p = p.next
        slow = slow.next
    return p
```

Why does that work? Name three distances, by convention with Greek letters: **μ** (mu) is the tail length from the head to the cycle's first node, **λ** (lambda) is the number of nodes in the cycle, and k is how far past the cycle's first node the pointers met. These count link steps and nodes, not memory addresses.

When they first meet, fast has walked twice as far as slow, yet they stand on the same node. Fast's extra distance must therefore be a whole number of laps. Slow's distance is the tail, some whole laps and then k more, which leads to the key relationship:

```formula essential
t = μ + k + jλ
2t − t = qλ
μ + k = (q − j)λ = mλ
where
t: the number of steps slow has taken when the pointers first meet; fast has taken 2t steps by then
μ: mu, the number of steps from the head to the first node of the cycle
k: how many steps past the cycle's first node the meeting point is (0 up to λ − 1)
λ: lambda, the number of nodes in the cycle
j: how many complete laps of the cycle slow made before meeting (0 or more)
q: how many whole laps fast is ahead of slow at the meeting
m: the whole number q − j (0 or more; it is 0 only when the cycle starts at the head and they meet there)
In words: fast's extra distance is a whole number of laps, so the tail length plus the meeting offset is a whole number of laps too.
```

The last line is the key. Walking μ steps forward from the meeting point means being μ + k steps past the cycle's start in total: a whole number of laps, so it lands exactly back on the start. Meanwhile a pointer walking μ steps from the head also arrives at the start. Both move one step at a time, so the first node where they meet is the cycle's start. The argument also covers a zero-length tail, where the cycle starts at the head; there the initial equality at the head is not treated as a detected cycle.

> [!example] Trace
> List `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> (back to 3)`: a two-step tail and a four-node cycle. Phase 1: slow visits 2, 3, 4, 5 while fast visits 3, 5, 3, 5. They meet at **5** after 4 steps, 2 steps into the cycle. Tail plus offset is four steps, exactly one lap. Phase 2: starting from 1 and 5, one step each gives (2, 6), then (3, 3). They meet at **3**, the cycle start, after two steps: the tail length.

To get the cycle's length, hold one pointer at the meeting point and walk the other round until it returns, counting steps.

The same idea finds a duplicate in an array of n + 1 values, each between 1 and n, treating each value as a "next" pointer. Brent's algorithm is a variant that typically does fewer pointer moves.

## Key takeaways
- At a meeting, the fast pointer has gained a whole number of cycle laps.
- Reset one pointer to the head and move both one link per step.

## Further reading
- [Cycle detection — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_detection)

options.explanation: The first meeting is usually somewhere inside the cycle. In `1→2→3→4→5→(2)` the pointers meet at node 5 while the cycle starts at node 2; phase 2 is what finds the start.

options.explanation: Neither the meeting offset nor the tail length is fixed. A tail of three nodes and a five-node cycle, for example, meet two nodes into the cycle.

options.text: Because the tail length plus the meeting offset is a whole number of laps, so walking the tail length from the meeting point lands on the start, just as walking it from the head does
options.explanation: Correct. At the meeting, fast's extra distance is whole laps, which forces tail plus offset to be whole laps. Both pointers need exactly the tail length in steps to reach the start, so they arrive together.

options.text: It only works when the tail is shorter than the cycle; otherwise the head pointer arrives first

questions.workedExample:

2. Slow walked the tail, possibly some whole laps, and then some offset past the cycle's first node. Since slow's total distance equals fast's extra distance, tail plus offset must also be a whole number of laps.
3. Phase 2: the pointer left at the meeting point is already the offset past the start. Walking the tail length more takes it to tail plus offset past the start, which is whole laps, so it lands exactly on the start.
4. The pointer reset to the head reaches the start after exactly the tail length too. Moving one step at a time, they first coincide at the start.
5. Example: a three-node tail and a five-node cycle meet two nodes into the cycle. Three plus two is five, one full lap, and three more steps from offset two wrap round to the start.

If phase 2 moved one pointer two steps at a time, the distances would no longer match and the pointers could meet elsewhere or not at the start.

lessons.title: Dummy heads and fixed-gap deletion
lessons.summary: A dummy supplies a predecessor even for the real head.
lessons.body:
Use the Node class from the reversal unit and assume a finite, acyclic list. Here n is the requested one-based distance from the end, rather than the list length. A temporary dummy node supplies a stable predecessor even when the target is the real head.

## Dummy heads

Many list operations treat the first node specially: deleting it changes `head`, and building a new list has no node to attach the first element to. A **dummy head** (a sentinel placed before the real head) removes the special case. Build or modify the list after the dummy, then return `dummy.next`.

### Removing the n-th node from the end

Use two pointers with a gap of n between them. When the front one hits the end, the back one is just before the target.

```python
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    if not isinstance(n, int) or n < 1:
        raise ValueError("n must be >= 1")
    # Give the real head a predecessor.
    dummy = Node(0, head)
    front = back = dummy
    # Keep back just before the target.
    for _ in range(n + 1):
        if front is None:
            raise ValueError("n too large")
        front = front.next
    while front:
        front = front.next
        back = back.next
    # Remove the target after validation.
    back.next = back.next.next
    return dummy.next
```

Without the dummy, removing the *first* node (when n equals the length) needs its own branch. With it, `back` simply stays at the dummy and the general code works.

### Trace the boundary cases

On the five-node chain with values one through five, requesting the last node leaves the back pointer at node four when front runs off the chain. Requesting the fifth node from the end keeps back at the dummy; bypassing its successor removes the real head with the same statement.

The extra initial step is intentional: back must end before the target, not on it. Advancing beyond the available chain raises the explicit error before any link is changed. An empty list has no valid positive removal distance. A zero or negative distance is rejected, rather than silently removing an unrelated node.

Python treats bool as an int subclass, so the shown isinstance check accepts True as distance one. Callers that must reject Boolean arguments need a stricter validation contract. This teaching example otherwise leaves all non-target node identities intact.

## Key takeaways
- A dummy supplies a predecessor even for the real head.
- Validate the requested position before bypassing a target.

## Further reading
- [Linked list — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linked_list)

lessons.title: Stable destructive merging and merge schedules
lessons.summary: Relink node-disjoint sorted inputs and attach an untouched suffix.
lessons.body:
Use the Node class from the reversal unit. A dummy node provides an initial attachment point, and the current output tail tells you where to append the next selected node. The inputs below must not share nodes: rewiring intersecting inputs can create a cycle.

## Merging two sorted lists

Assume two sorted, acyclic, node-disjoint lists and constant-time value comparison. This destructive merge repeatedly takes the smaller head and attaches it to the result. A dummy head gives you somewhere to attach the first node.

```python
def merge(a, b):
    dummy = tail = Node(0)
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            # Attach A before advancing its
            # input.
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            # Attach B before advancing its
            # input.
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b   # leftovers
    return dummy.next
```

```
a: 1 -> 4 -> 6
b: 2 -> 3 -> 7
take 1(a) 2(b) 3(b) 4(a) 6(a)
a empty: attach rest of b (7)
result: 1 2 3 4 6 7
```

For lists of n and m nodes, this is O(n + m) time and O(1) extra space: it relinks existing nodes rather than creating new ones. Using `<=` keeps equal elements in their original order (a **stable merge**), which matters for merge sort.

Merge is the core of **merge sort on linked lists**, which is the standard way to sort an n-node list in O(n log n) without random access (log n is log₂ n, the number of times n can be halved before reaching 1; it is how many levels of splitting there are): find the middle with fast/slow pointers, split, sort each half, merge.

### Several sorted lists

Sequentially merging each new list into the whole accumulated result keeps re-walking the earlier nodes: the first list's nodes take part in every merge. Balanced pairwise rounds instead halve the number of lists each round, and every round touches each node once, so each node takes part in only as many merges as there are halving rounds.

```formula reference
W_seq ≈ kN / 2
W_pair = N log_2(k)
where
W_seq: cumulative merge-input size in a sequential schedule, in nodes
W_pair: cumulative merge-input size for balanced pairwise rounds, in nodes; the equality assumes a power-of-two list count and equal-length lists
N: total nodes across all lists
k: number of lists, at least two
log_2: base-two logarithm, giving the halving-round count
≈: approximate equality omitting lower-order terms
In words: sequential merging grows with the number of lists times the total size, while balanced rounds grow with the total size times the number of halving rounds, which is far smaller when there are many lists.
```

For eight lists of one thousand nodes each, sequential merging handles thirty-five thousand node inputs in total; three balanced rounds handle twenty-four thousand. The gap widens quickly as the list count grows. Actual comparisons can be fewer because merge attaches an untouched suffix. For non-power-of-two list counts, balanced round counts are rounded up and some lists sit out a round. A heap of current heads also gives O(N log k), with N and k as defined above, but its mechanics belong to the later heaps module.

## Key takeaways
- Relink node-disjoint sorted inputs and attach an untouched suffix.
- Balanced pairwise rounds avoid repeatedly scanning an ever-growing result.

## Further reading
- [Linked list — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linked_list)
- [Merge sort — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merge_sort)

lessons.title: Combine pointer patterns and preserve caller state
lessons.summary: Split, reverse and compare can test a palindrome with fixed extra space.
lessons.body:
The previous units established reversal, middle finding, fixed gaps and merging. Combine these patterns without changing their assumptions: ordinary traversal and intersection search below require finite, acyclic inputs. In the complexity bounds n is the number of nodes being processed.

## Combining patterns

Harder problems chain these together.

- **Is the list a palindrome, in O(1) space?** Find the middle (fast/slow), reverse the second half, compare the two halves node by node, then reverse it back to restore the list.
- **Reorder `1,2,3,4,5` to `1,5,2,4,3`?** Find the middle, reverse the second half, then interleave the halves.
- **Where do two lists intersect?** Walk pointer A along list A then list B, and pointer B along B then A. Both travel the same total distance, so they arrive at the shared node together (or both reach `None`).

> [!warning] Common bugs
> - Losing the rest of the list by overwriting `next` before saving it.
> - Checking `fast.next.next` without first checking `fast.next`, causing an AttributeError on short lists.
> - Comparing values (`==`) when you mean identity (`is`).
> - Forgetting to restore a list you mutated (for example in the palindrome check), surprising the caller.

### Intersection by switching routes

Use node identity and finite acyclic inputs. Each pointer traverses its own list, then switches to the other head on the iteration after it reaches None. Equal total routes cancel out the difference between the two unshared prefixes. If there is no shared node, both eventually reach None together.

```python
def intersection(a, b):
    p, q = a, b
    while p is not q:
        # Switch heads after the null state.
        p = p.next if p else b
        q = q.next if q else a
    # Shared node, or None for no junction.
    return p
```

For distinct prefixes of three and five nodes followed by four shared nodes, the pointers meet after thirteen loop iterations. One pointer traverses seven links to None, spends one iteration switching, then traverses the other five-node prefix. The other traverses nine links, switches, and takes three more. Equal-length inputs can meet earlier; count the extra iteration spent on None when tracing this exact loop.

For the palindrome pattern, split so the second half excludes an odd middle node, reverse that second half, compare corresponding values, and reverse it back even after a mismatch. Restoring the original links is part of the function’s contract, rather than an optional cosmetic step. An implementation must also reconnect any link it detached during splitting.

## Key takeaways
- Split, reverse and compare can test a palindrome with fixed extra space.
- Switching to the other list's head equalises the two intersection-search routes, including the step through None.

## Further reading
- [Cycle detection — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cycle_detection)
- [Linked list — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linked_list)

Two lists share a tail. List A has 3 nodes of its own, then the 4 shared nodes; list B has 5 of its own, then the same 4. How many loop iterations until `p is q`?


Correct. p takes 7 iterations to step past A's 7 nodes to None, 1 iteration to switch to B's head, then 5 more to cross B's unique nodes onto the first shared node: 13. q takes 9 + 1 + 3 = 13 too.
Close: the hops through the unshared nodes and one list's shared part add up to 12, but each pointer also spends one iteration switching from `None` to the other list's head.

options.explanation: Switching lists is exactly what equalises the distances: both travel the same total to the junction: A's own nodes, plus B's own nodes, plus the shared nodes, plus the one iteration spent switching from None to the other head.

questions.workedExample:
The unique prefixes have three and five nodes; the shared suffix has four.

1. Pointer p reaches None after traversing A's seven nodes: seven iterations.
2. Iteration 8: p switches to b's head.
3. Five more iterations through B's unique nodes: iteration 13 lands on the first shared node.
4. Pointer q takes nine iterations to reach None, switches to A's head on iteration ten, and needs three more to reach the shared node on iteration thirteen.

options.text: Compare the first half with the reversed second half node by node

lessons.title: Stack operations and storage choices
lessons.summary: LIFO uses the newest item first.
lessons.body:
A **stack** is a collection where you can only touch the top. You add to the top (**push**) and remove from the top (**pop**), so the last thing in is the first thing out: **LIFO**.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A pile of plates
> In a pile of clean plates you put new plates on top and take plates from the top. The plate you washed last is the first one you use.
>
> **How it maps:** Putting a plate on is `push`, taking the top plate is `pop`, glancing at it is `peek`, and the plate at the bottom is the oldest item, which leaves last: LIFO.
>
> **Where it stops:** You could physically slide a plate out of the middle; a stack's interface forbids it. A dynamic-array stack also has a capacity that grows by copying, which a pile of plates never needs.

That restriction sounds limiting, but it is exactly the shape of a huge number of problems: anything nested, anything you need to undo in reverse order, and anything where the most recent item is the one that matters.

## The operations

| Operation | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `push(x)` | Put x on top | O(1) amortised on a dynamic array |
| `pop()` | Remove and return the top | O(1) amortised on a dynamic array |
| `peek()` | Return the top without removing | O(1) |
| `is_empty()` | Any items left? | O(1) |

Popping or peeking an empty stack is an error (a **stack underflow**). Pushing onto a full fixed-size stack is a **stack overflow**.

```
push 1, push 2, push 3, pop

 |   |     |   |     | 3 |     |   |
 |   |     | 2 |     | 2 |     | 2 |
 | 1 |     | 1 |     | 1 |     | 1 |
 +---+     +---+     +---+     +---+
                          pop -> 3
```

## Implementations

### On a dynamic array

Keep the top at the **end** of the array, so push and pop never shift anything. In Python, a list already is a stack:

```python
stack = []
stack.append(1)    # push
stack.append(2)
top = stack[-1]    # peek -> 2
stack.pop()        # pop  -> 2
if not stack:      # empty check
    ...
```

Push and pop are amortised O(1) in CPython (growth or shrinking can resize the pointer array), and the list’s reference slots are contiguous, so this is fast in practice.

Putting the top at the *front* (`insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)`) would make every operation O(n) on a stack of n items, because every other item shifts. Always grow stacks at the cheap end.

### On a linked list

Push and pop at the **head**:

```python
class LinkedStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None

    def push(self, x):
        self.head = Node(x, self.head)

    def pop(self):
        if self.head is None:
            raise IndexError("empty")
        x = self.head.val
        # Expose the next item as the new
        # top.
        self.head = self.head.next
        return x
```

Each operation uses O(1) pointer updates and there is never a resize, assuming constant-time node allocation and reclamation in the data-structure model. The cost is a heap allocation per push and worse cache behaviour.

A linked stack is also the basis of the classic **lock-free stack** (the Treiber stack): push and pop retry compare-and-swap on the head until successful. Lock-free progress is not bounded per-thread latency, and safe memory reclamation/ABA handling requires care.

### In the standard libraries

- **Python:** use `list`. (`collections.deque` also works; `queue.LifoQueue` adds thread-safe blocking, which you only need between threads.)
- **Java:** use `ArrayDeque` via the `Deque` interface (`push`, `pop`, `peek`). The old `java.util.Stack` extends `Vector`, so it inherits synchronized methods and it exposes index-based methods that break the stack abstraction. Oracle's docs recommend `Deque` instead.
- **C++:** `std::stack` is an adaptor over another container, `std::deque` by default (you can choose `std::vector`).

## Key takeaways
- LIFO uses the newest item first.
- Place the top at an array end or linked-list head to avoid shifting.

## Further reading
- [Stack (abstract data type) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(abstract_data_type))
- [Deque — Java SE 21 API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Deque.html)
- [Using lists as stacks — Python tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html)

questions.prompt: You need a stack in new single-threaded Java code. Which choice is recommended?

options.text: `java.util.Stack`
options.explanation: `Stack` is a legacy class that extends `Vector`: many methods are synchronized (unneeded locking for this case), and it exposes index access like `get(i)` that breaks LIFO discipline. Its own docs point you to `Deque`.

options.text: `LinkedList` used with `add` and `remove(0)`
options.explanation: `LinkedList` can serve as a stack via `Deque` methods, but allocates a node per push. And `add` appends at the tail while `remove(0)` removes the head: that's FIFO, a queue.

options.text: `ArrayList` with `add(0, x)` and `remove(0)`
options.explanation: Using index 0 as the top shifts every element on each push and pop: O(n). If you use an ArrayList, push and pop at the end.

options.text: `ArrayDeque` through the `Deque` interface (`push`, `pop`, `peek`)
options.explanation: Correct. It's a resizable circular array: O(1) amortised at both ends, no locking, good cache behaviour. The Javadoc says it's likely faster than `Stack` when used as a stack.

questions.workedExample:
```java
Deque<Integer> st =
    new ArrayDeque<>();
st.push(1);   // addFirst
st.push(2);
st.peek();    // 2
st.pop();     // 2
```

1. `push`/`pop`/`peek` operate on the head of the deque.
2. `ArrayDeque` is backed by a circular array, so these are O(1) amortised with no shifting. (An `ArrayList` used at index 0 would shift all n stored elements on every push and pop: O(n).)
3. No synchronisation cost, unlike `Stack`/`Vector`.
4. One gotcha: `ArrayDeque` rejects `null` elements.

questions.prompt: You compare a stack built on a Python `list` with one built on a singly linked list (push/pop at the head). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The linked version gives worst-case O(1) push, while the list's push is O(1) only amortised
options.explanation: Correct. A list push that triggers a resize copies every pointer: O(n) for that one push. A linked push never copies the existing sequence; constant-time allocation is assumed by this model.

options.text: The list version is usually faster in practice, thanks to contiguous storage and no per-push allocation
options.explanation: Correct. Each linked push allocates a node object; the list writes into spare capacity. Resizes are rare and cheap per element.

options.text: Implementing the list stack with `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` is equally efficient
options.explanation: Incorrect. Operating at index 0 shifts every element, making each operation O(n). Always use the end of an array as the top.

options.text: A linked stack is the basis of the classic lock-free (Treiber) stack, where push and pop swap the head pointer with compare-and-swap
options.explanation: Correct. CAS updates the shared head, retrying on interference. Safe publication, ABA prevention and reclamation also matter; the teaching linked stack itself is not concurrent.

options.text: Both use the same amount of memory per element
options.explanation: Incorrect. The list needs one pointer per element (plus spare capacity); the linked version needs a whole node object per element, with its own header and `next` pointer.

questions.workedExample:
1. Worst case vs amortised, for a stack of n items: an occasional list push finds the array full and copies all n references, O(n) for that push. CPython's growth is geometric (about an eighth extra each time), so those copies are spread thinly and the average stays O(1). A linked push is always: allocate node, set `next`, move head.
2. Practice: allocation and pointer chasing dominate, so `list.append`/`pop` wins in CPython for typical sizes.
3. Linked nodes avoid resize copies, but hard real-time use still needs bounded allocation/reclamation and scheduling. Lock-free stacks require a dedicated concurrent algorithm; this Python class is not one.
4. Never put the top at index 0 of an array.

lessons.title: Call frames and balanced nesting
lessons.summary: A call frame retains the state needed after a nested call returns.
lessons.body:
A stack serves the last added item first. Nested function calls and nested bracket pairs both require the most recent unfinished task to finish first. For the bracket checker n is the input character count; for call frames depth is the number of active nested calls.

## The call stack

In the ordinary unoptimised call-stack model, each active call has a **stack frame** retaining its arguments, local state and a **return address** (where to continue when it finishes). Returning releases that frame. Registers, inlining, tail calls and runtime-managed frames can change the physical layout.

```python
def a(): return b() + 1
def b(): return c() * 2
def c(): return 5
a()
```

```
call a     call b     call c     c returns 5
+-----+    +-----+    +-----+    +-----+
|     |    |     |    |  c  |    |     |
|     |    |  b  |    |  b  |    |  b  |
|  a  |    |  a  |    |  a  |    |  a  |
+-----+    +-----+    +-----+    +-----+
```

This is why recursion uses O(depth) memory, and why unbounded recursion fails:

- Native thread stacks have implementation- and configuration-dependent limits. Excessive native recursion can exhaust them, often causing a fault; Java can raise StackOverflowError. Compiler optimizations and runtime-managed frames can change this simple model.
- CPython guards itself with a recursion limit (commonly **1,000** at startup), raising `RecursionError`; inspect `sys.getrecursionlimit()` for the actual process setting.

Any recursive algorithm can be rewritten with an **explicit stack** on the heap, which can grow to gigabytes. Depth-first search on a large graph is the usual example (see the graphs module).

## Balanced brackets

Is `{[()()]}` balanced? Is `([)]`? Nesting means the most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed: a stack.

```python
def balanced(s):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in "([{":
            # Remember the latest unmatched
            # opener.
            stack.append(ch)
        elif ch in pairs:
            if not stack:
                return False
            # A closer must match that
            # newest opener.
            if stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
                return False
    return not stack
```

Three ways to fail:

1. A closer that doesn't match the top: `([)]` fails at `)`, because the top is `[`.
2. A closer with an empty stack: `())`.
3. Openers left over at the end: `((`.

For a string of n characters, that is O(n) time, and O(n) space in the worst case (a string of nothing but openers). Compilers, linters, JSON and XML parsers and your editor's bracket matching all use this idea.

> [!tip] One bracket type?
> If there's only `(` and `)`, you don't need the stack itself, just a counter: +1 for `(`, −1 for `)`, fail if it goes negative, and require 0 at the end.

## Key takeaways
- A call frame retains the state needed after a nested call returns.
- Each closer must match the newest unfinished opener.

## Further reading
- [Call stack — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_stack)
- [Using lists as stacks — Python tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html)

options.text: In the ordinary unoptimized call-stack model, each call pushes a frame with its arguments, locals and return address; returning pops it
options.explanation: Correct. That's what lets a function resume exactly where it left off after a nested call returns.

options.text: With constant-size frames and no tail-call elimination, recursive depth d uses O(d) stack memory
options.explanation: Correct. Every pending call holds a frame until it returns.

options.text: In CPython, exceeding the recursion limit (configured as 1,000 in this example) raises `RecursionError`
options.explanation: Correct. The interpreter enforces a configured recursion-depth guard. Python frames and native C-stack use differ across versions.

2. With the recursion limit configured as 1,000, a straightforward five-thousand-level recursive factorial exceeds it and raises RecursionError.
3. Without optimisation, C recursion can exhaust a configured native thread stack. A guard-page fault is common, but the stack layout, protection and resulting failure depend on the platform.
4. Fix: an explicit stack, e.g. an iterative graph traversal. (This version marks nodes when pushed, so it visits every reachable node once but does not always reproduce recursive depth-first order.)

```python
stack = [start]
seen = {start}
while stack:
    node = stack.pop()
    for nb in graph[node]:
        if nb not in seen:
            seen.add(nb)
            stack.append(nb)
```

lessons.title: Evaluate postfix expressions with a stack
lessons.summary: Push operands and replace the last two with each operator result.
lessons.body:
A stack removes its newest value first. In postfix notation that value is the right operand of a binary operator, and the next value is the left operand. This is a teaching evaluator for numeric tokens, not a complete expression parser.

## Evaluating expressions

### Postfix (Reverse Polish notation)

In **postfix** notation, operators come after their operands: `3 4 +` means 3 + 4. There are no brackets and no precedence rules, and evaluation is a single stack pass:

- Number: push it.
- Operator: pop two values, apply, push the result.

```python
def eval_rpn(tokens):
    stack = []
    for t in tokens:
        if t in {"+", "-", "*", "/"}:
            b = stack.pop()  # right
            a = stack.pop()  # left
            if t == "+":
                stack.append(a + b)
            elif t == "-":
                stack.append(a - b)
            elif t == "*":
                stack.append(a * b)
            else:
                stack.append(a / b)
        else:
            # Operand tokens wait for their
            # operator.
            stack.append(float(t))
    if len(stack) != 1:
        raise ValueError("malformed RPN")
    return stack.pop()
```

This teaching evaluator expects numeric tokens and binary operators. Missing operands raise IndexError; invalid numeric tokens raise ValueError. It uses floating-point arithmetic.

Note the pop order: the **first** pop is the **right** operand. Getting it backwards breaks `-` and `/`.

```
5 1 2 + 4 * + 3 -

token  stack
5      [5]
1      [5, 1]
2      [5, 1, 2]
+      [5, 3]
4      [5, 3, 4]
*      [5, 12]
+      [17]
3      [17, 3]
-      [14]
```

HP calculators, the PostScript language, the JVM's bytecode and CPython's bytecode interpreter are all stack machines that work this way.

### Trace the operand contract

For the tokens `10 4 -`, push ten, then four. The first pop is four, the right operand; the second is ten, the left operand. Subtracting in that order returns six. For `8 2 /`, the same rule returns four. Reversing the order would return negative six and one quarter respectively.

The example deliberately leaves several malformed-input errors visible. An operator with too few operands raises IndexError. A nonnumeric operand token raises ValueError during float conversion. Two leftover values raise the final malformed-expression error. Division by zero raises ZeroDivisionError. A production parser would catch and present these errors with token positions.

Each token is processed once, so evaluation is linear in the token count when token conversion and arithmetic costs are treated as fixed. The stack can hold a linear number of operands. Very large numeric tokens, precision requirements and arbitrary-precision arithmetic need their own cost and representation model.

## Key takeaways
- Push operands and replace the last two with each operator result.
- The first popped value is the right operand.

## Further reading
- [Reverse Polish notation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_Polish_notation)

The same swapped order affects both operators. Subtraction is wrong too: 4 − 10 = −6.

lessons.title: Precedence and associativity with shunting-yard
lessons.summary: Hold operators until their operands and precedence permit output.
lessons.body:
Postfix evaluation needs no operator-precedence rule because each operator follows its operands. To convert ordinary infix text, keep a separate stack of pending operators while emitting the operand order. The conversion trace below concerns expression tokens, not Python source.

### Infix to postfix: the shunting-yard algorithm

Humans write **infix** (`3 + 4 * 2`). Edsger Dijkstra's **shunting-yard algorithm** converts it to postfix using a stack of pending operators:

- Operand: send straight to the output.
- `(`: push.
- `)`: pop operators to the output until the matching `(`; discard both brackets.
- Operator `o`: while the top of the stack is an operator with **higher** precedence, or **equal** precedence and `o` is left-associative, pop it to the output. Then push `o`.
- At the end, pop everything left.

```
3 + 4 * 2

token  output      ops
3      3
+      3           +
4      3 4         +
*      3 4         + *   (* beats +)
2      3 4 2       + *
end    3 4 2 * +
```

The result, `3 4 2 * +`, evaluates to 11, respecting precedence. Associativity matters too: `a - b - c` becomes `a b - c -` (left to right), while exponentiation is right-associative, so `2 ^ 3 ^ 2` becomes `2 3 2 ^ ^`. Grouping from the right gives a very different answer from grouping from the left:

```formula reference
2 ^ 3 ^ 2 = 2 ^ (3 ^ 2) = 2 ^ 9 = 512
(2 ^ 3) ^ 2 = 8 ^ 2 = 64
where
^: raised to the power of: 2 ^ 3 means 2 × 2 × 2 = 8
In words: grouping from the right first raises 3 to the power 2, giving 9, and then raises 2 to the power 9, giving 512. Grouping from the left would instead square 8 and give 64, so the associativity rule changes the answer.
```

Python's `**` follows the same convention: `2 ** 3 ** 2 == 512`.

### Equal precedence is the deciding test

Precedence alone cannot decide `a - b - c`, because both operators have the same precedence. Associativity breaks the tie. Subtraction groups from the left, so when the second `-` arrives it first pops the pending `-`: the first subtraction finishes before the second starts its right operand. With `10 - 4 - 2` that gives (10 − 4) − 2, which is 4; grouping from the right would wrongly give 8. A right-associative operator such as `^` does the opposite: an equal-precedence `^` already on the stack stays there, waiting for the right-hand exponent.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A railway shunting yard
> The algorithm is named after a railway shunting yard because it works like one. Wagons arrive in one order, and some are pushed into a dead-end siding to wait while others go straight through to the departing train. A wagon parked last in the siding is the first to come back out.
>
> **How it maps:** Operands are wagons that go straight to the output train. Operators are parked in the siding, which is the operator stack, and leave it, newest first, when an incoming operator of lower precedence (or equal precedence and left-associative) or a closing bracket requires them to.
>
> **Where it stops:** A real siding has no rules about which wagon outranks another; precedence and associativity are what make the algorithm work. Brackets also have no railway counterpart: they act as markers inside the siding that stop operators being released too early.

The conversion handles each token once and each operator is pushed and popped at most once. This gives linear total stack work in the token count, assuming fixed-time token classification. The displayed rules describe binary operators; unary minus, functions and argument separators require additional grammar rules.

## Key takeaways
- Hold operators until their operands and precedence permit output.
- Equal precedence pops for left associativity but waits for right associativity.

## Further reading
- [Shunting yard algorithm — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shunting_yard_algorithm)
- [Reverse Polish notation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_Polish_notation)

lessons.title: Monotonic stacks and total-work counting
lessons.summary: Unresolved indices wait until a later value supplies their answer.
lessons.body:
The preceding stack units used last-in, first-out storage. Here the stack additionally keeps unresolved candidates in nonincreasing value order. In every bound n is the number of input values; equal values may remain together because only a strictly larger value answers the query.

## The monotonic stack

A **monotonic stack** keeps its contents in sorted order (all increasing or all decreasing) by popping anything that would break the order before each push. It solves "for each element, find the nearest element to the left or right that is bigger (or smaller)" in O(n).

**Next greater element:** for each value, find the first larger value to its right.

```python
def next_greater(nums):
    res = [-1] * len(nums)
    stack = []  # indices; values decrease
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:
            # This waiting index has found
            # its answer.
            res[stack.pop()] = x
        # The new index now waits for a
        # larger one.
        stack.append(i)
    return res

next_greater([2, 1, 2, 4, 3])
# [4, 2, 4, -1, -1]
```

The stack holds indices still **waiting** for a bigger value. When `x` arrives, every waiting element smaller than `x` has found its answer and is popped.

There's a `while` inside a `for`, but for n input values it's still **O(n)**. Instead of asking how long one `while` loop can run, count the work over the whole run: every index is pushed exactly once, can be popped at most once, and each pass of the `for` loop ends its `while` loop with one failed check.

```formula reference
events = pushes + pops + exits
events ≤ n + n + n = 3n
where
events: counted push events, pop events and final failed while checks; a successful while check is charged together with its ensuing pop, not counted separately
n: the number of input values
pushes: exactly n, one per index
pops: at most n, because each index can be popped only once after being pushed once
exits: exactly n: each pass of the for loop ends its while loop once, when the check fails
≤: is less than or equal to
In words: however the pops are spread out, the whole run does at most three counted events per input value, each taking fixed work, so the total is linear. This is a counting bound, not an exact count of Python instructions.
```

One step can pop many items, but then other steps pop none: for `[2, 1, 2, 4, 3]` the 4 pops two waiting indices at once, while three of the five steps pop nothing. This is an **amortised** argument, like dynamic array growth.

The same pattern answers "how many days until a warmer temperature", stock span problems and the largest rectangle in a histogram.

## Other uses

- **Undo** in editors: push each action; undo pops it. Redo is a second stack.
- **Browser back button:** a stack of visited pages.
- **Backtracking** (maze solving, Sudoku): push choices, pop to retreat.
- **Parsers:** compilers use a stack to track nested constructs.

## Key takeaways
- Unresolved indices wait until a later value supplies their answer.
- Count pushes and pops over the complete run rather than multiplying the inner and outer loop bounds.

## Further reading
- [Stack (abstract data type) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack_(abstract_data_type))

lessons.title: FIFO queues and the cost of front shifting
lessons.summary: A queue serves arrivals in their original order.
lessons.body:
A **queue** adds items at the back and removes them from the front. The first one in is the first one out: **FIFO**. Where a stack serves the most recent arrival, a queue serves the one that has waited longest.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A line at a shop counter
> People join the back of the line and the cashier serves whoever is at the front. In a narrow corridor, every time someone is served, everyone behind them shuffles one step forward.
>
> **How it maps:** Joining is `enqueue`, being served is `dequeue`, and the first to arrive is the first to leave. The shuffling corridor is a Python list used with `pop(0)`: every removal moves all the remaining items one slot. A better design keeps people still and moves a "now serving" marker instead, which is what a circular buffer does.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real people can give up and leave from the middle, or be let in early; a plain FIFO queue does not allow either. People shuffle forward all at once, so the line advances in one moment however long it is; a computer moves the items one after another, so `pop(0)` takes time proportional to the number still waiting.

Queues are everywhere in real systems. Print jobs, network packets in a router, tasks waiting for a thread pool, messages in broker partitions or queue services, keystrokes waiting for your program to read them: all queues. Inside algorithms, the queue is what makes **breadth-first search** explore nearest-first.

## The operations

| Operation | What it does | Target cost |
|---|---|---|
| `enqueue(x)` | Add x at the back | O(1) |
| `dequeue()` | Remove from the front | O(1) |
| `peek()` | Look at the front | O(1) |
| `is_empty()` | Anything waiting? | O(1) |

```
dequeue <- [ A | B | C | D ] <- enqueue
          front           back
```

## The wrong way: a plain list

The obvious Python queue is a list with `append` and `pop(0)`:

```python
q = []
q.append("A")   # enqueue, O(1)
q.pop(0)        # dequeue, O(n)!
```

`pop(0)` shifts every remaining element one slot left. Draining a queue of n items this way moves n − 1 elements on the first dequeue, n − 2 on the next, and so on down to 0:

```formula reference
moves = n(n − 1) / 2
where
moves: the total number of element moves to empty the queue
n: the number of items in the queue at the start
In words: each dequeue shifts everything still waiting, so the total grows with the square of the queue length: about half of n squared.
```

For 100,000 items that is about five billion moves, where a proper queue would do 100,000 cheap operations. That is O(n²) for the whole drain, or O(n) per dequeue. The bug is invisible in tests with 10 items and catastrophic in production with a million.

Two structures fix it: a linked list with head and tail pointers (dequeue at the head, enqueue at the tail, both O(1)), or, usually better, a **circular buffer**.

## Key takeaways
- A queue serves arrivals in their original order.
- Repeated list-front removal shifts a quadratic total of elements.

## Further reading
- [collections.deque — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)
- [ArrayDeque — Java SE 21 API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/ArrayDeque.html)

lessons.title: Ring-buffer indices and constant pointer work
lessons.summary: Wrap the next write slot round after the physical array end.
lessons.body:
FIFO removal should advance a front position rather than shift all waiting elements. A fixed ring keeps a positive capacity and a live count. The example assumes single-threaded access; adding concurrent producers or consumers needs a separate synchronisation protocol.

## Circular buffers

A **circular buffer** (ring buffer) is a fixed array whose end wraps round to its start. Track the index of the front (`head`) and the number of items (`count`). When the buffer is not full, the next free slot at the back is `count` places after `head`, wrapping round to slot 0 when it runs off the end:

```formula reference
back = (head + count) mod capacity
where
back: the slot index where the next enqueued item is written
head: the slot index of the item at the front (the next to be dequeued)
count: how many items are in the buffer now
capacity: the number of slots in the array
mod: modulo: the remainder after dividing; 6 mod 4 = 2. It makes indices wrap round, so they always stay between 0 and capacity − 1. Python writes it %
In words: start at the front, step forward one slot per stored item, and wrap round to the start of the array when you pass the end.
```

With capacity 4, the front item in slot 2 and one item stored, the next item goes in slot 3; the one after that wraps round to slot 0, back at the start of the array. In Python this is `(head + count) % capacity`.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Hours on a clock face
> On a 12-hour clock, five hours after 10 o'clock is 3 o'clock, not 15 o'clock: the count wraps round past 12 and starts again.
>
> **How it maps:** The clock positions are the buffer's slots, the current hour is `head`, and counting forward `count` hours finds the back. Wrapping past 12 is the wrap-round step (`% capacity` in Python) that keeps every index inside the array.
>
> **Where it stops:** A clock has no notion of empty or full slots, and its numbers run 1 to 12, whereas array slots are numbered from 0 up to one less than the capacity. The buffer must also refuse a write when every slot is in use, which the next unit covers.

Dequeuing just advances `head`. Nothing shifts.

```
capacity 4. enqueue A B C,
dequeue twice, enqueue D E F:

slot:   0   1   2   3
       [E | F | C | D]
                ^ head = 2
dequeue order: C, D, E, F
```

```python
class RingQueue:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        valid = isinstance(cap, int)
        if not valid or cap < 1:
            raise ValueError("cap >= 1")
        self.buf = [None] * cap
        self.cap = cap
        self.head = 0
        self.count = 0

    def enqueue(self, x):
        if self.count == self.cap:
            raise OverflowError("full")
        n = self.head + self.count
        # Wrap the next write slot at
        # capacity.
        i = n % self.cap
        # Write into the free logical back
        # slot.
        self.buf[i] = x
        self.count += 1

    def dequeue(self):
        if self.count == 0:
            raise IndexError("empty")
        h = self.head
        x = self.buf[h]
        self.buf[h] = None   # drop the ref
        # Advance the front without
        # shifting.
        self.head = (h + 1) % self.cap
        self.count -= 1
        return x
```

## Key takeaways
- Wrap the next write slot round after the physical array end.
- Clear a dequeued slot so its old object need not stay alive.

## Further reading
- [Circular buffer — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_buffer)

lessons.title: Full ring buffers and bounded overload
lessons.summary: A count, reserved slot or monotonic counters distinguishes full from empty.
lessons.body:
The preceding unit implemented a ring with a count. Alternative representations must still distinguish its full and empty states. This unit connects capacity policy to overload: accepting work faster than it can be completed builds a backlog regardless of how cheap an enqueue is.

### Full or empty?

If you store `head` and `tail` indices instead of a count, `head == tail` is ambiguous: it is true both when the buffer is empty and when it is full. The usual fixes:

1. Keep a **count** (as above).
2. **Waste one slot**: declare the buffer full when `(tail + 1) % cap == head`, so a full buffer holds one fewer item than the physical slot count and `head == tail` can only mean empty.
3. Use ever-increasing head and tail counters and compare `tail - head` with the capacity, taking indices `% cap` only when touching the array.

Use nonnegative logical counters for this model; fixed-width machine counters need an explicit wraparound and overflow protocol. Option 3 with a **power-of-two** capacity lets you replace `% cap` with a cheap **bit mask** `& (cap - 1)`:

```formula reference
i mod cap = band(i, cap − 1)
where
i: an ever-increasing head or tail counter
cap: the buffer capacity, which must be a power of two (2, 4, 8, 16, ...)
mod: modulo: the remainder after dividing by cap
band: the bitwise AND function: compares two numbers bit by bit, keeping a 1 only where both have a 1. Written & in C, Java and Python
In words: when the capacity is a power of two, the remainder after dividing by it is just the counter's lowest bits, which a single cheap bitwise AND instruction extracts. With any other capacity the shortcut gives wrong slots.
```

For example, with eight slots, counter 13 (binary 1101) masked with 7 (binary 0111) keeps 0101, slot 5, the same as the remainder of 13 divided by 8. The Linux kernel's `kfifo` relies on this, which is why it rounds sizes to powers of two.

### Growing and bounding

A ring buffer can grow like a dynamic array: allocate double the space and copy the items across in queue order, "unwrapping" them. Java ArrayDeque also grows a circular array, but OpenJDK 21 roughly doubles small buffers and grows larger ones by about 50%, with additional adjustments for required capacity.

Often you don't want it to grow. A bounded queue configured to block or reject producers provides **backpressure**: when consumers fall behind, producers block or are refused, instead of memory growing until the process dies. Audio drivers, network card receive rings and high-throughput designs like the LMAX Disruptor all use fixed-size rings.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A restaurant with a small waiting area
> A busy restaurant has a few chairs by the door. When the chairs are full, the host asks new arrivals to wait outside or come back later instead of packing the lobby until nobody can move.
>
> **How it maps:** The chairs are the bounded buffer, the kitchen is the consumer, and arriving diners are producers. Turning people away or making them wait outside is backpressure: blocking or rejecting `put` once the queue is full.
>
> **Where it stops:** A full waiting area does not make the kitchen cook faster; only more cooks, simpler dishes or fewer diners change throughput. Diners may also give up and leave, whereas a blocked producer thread simply waits unless it was given a timeout.

### Arrival rate versus service rate

With five thousand arrivals and one thousand completions per second, an unbounded queue accumulates four thousand extra items every second. After ten minutes it holds about 2.4 million items if the rates stay constant and it started empty. A new item behind that backlog waits about forty minutes at the same consumer rate.

Blocking or rejecting producers at a finite capacity prevents unlimited queue storage, but it does not make consumers faster. Improving throughput requires more service capacity, batching, or reducing accepted work. Storing backlog on disk changes the storage limit and durability policy rather than the basic rate imbalance.

## Key takeaways
- A count, reserved slot or monotonic counters distinguishes full from empty.
- A bound exposes overload but does not increase consumer throughput.

## Further reading
- [Circular buffer — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_buffer)
- [ArrayDeque — Java SE 21 API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/ArrayDeque.html)
- [Linux — circular-buffer conventions](https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/circular-buffers.html)

questions.workedExample:

Two fill levels must share a gap, and they are empty and full, both with a gap of 0.
3. Fix A: track `count`. Empty: count == 0. Full: count == cap.
4. Fix B: treat `(tail + 1) % cap == head` as full, so you only ever store cap − 1 items and a gap of 0 always means empty.

questions.prompt: A web scraper's producer thread finds 5,000 URLs per second and puts them on an **unbounded** `queue.Queue()`; consumer threads can fetch only 1,000 per second. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The queue grows by about 4,000 items per second until the process runs out of memory
options.explanation: Correct. Arrivals exceed departures by 4,000/s, so without a bound the backlog grows linearly: 14.4 million items per hour.

options.text: Using `queue.Queue(maxsize=10_000)` makes `put` block when it's full, slowing the producer to the consumers' pace
options.explanation: Correct. This is backpressure: the bounded queue pushes the slowdown upstream instead of absorbing it as memory.

options.text: Switching to `collections.deque` would solve the problem, because it's faster
options.explanation: Incorrect. Speed of the queue isn't the bottleneck; the consumers are. A faster unbounded queue grows just as quickly.

options.text: A bounded queue alone doesn't make the consumers faster; you still need more consumers, or to drop or sample work, to keep up
options.explanation: Correct. Bounding protects memory and makes overload visible, but throughput is set by the consumers.

options.text: Item latency stays constant because the queue is FIFO
options.explanation: Incorrect. With a growing backlog, each new URL waits behind everything queued before it, so latency climbs steadily.

questions.workedExample:
1. The backlog grows at the difference between the two rates: 5,000 arriving minus 1,000 leaving is 4,000 extra items every second.
2. After 10 minutes that is about 2.4 million queued URLs. If each takes about 200 bytes plus object overhead, that's hundreds of MB and climbing until memory runs out.
3. Latency: a newly arriving item has everything ahead of it to drain at 1,000 per second. Behind 2.4 million items that is about 2,400 seconds, 40 minutes, and the wait keeps growing.
4. `Queue(maxsize=N)`: `put` blocks when full (or raises `queue.Full` with `block=False`), so the producer slows to the consumers' 1,000 per second. That is backpressure.
5. Real fixes for throughput: more consumers, batching, or shedding load. Switching to `deque` only makes enqueueing cheaper, not consuming faster. Message brokers like Kafka and SQS can persist a backlog to disk, but the same rate imbalance still applies.

lessons.title: Deques, block layouts and bounded histories
lessons.summary: A deque supports both ends; its middle-access cost depends on implementation.
lessons.body:
A queue adds at one end and removes at the other. A deque allows either operation at either end. Here n is the number of stored items; bounds concern container operations, excluding user-defined finalisers or other work triggered by dropping an object.

## Deques: both ends

A **deque** (double-ended queue, pronounced "deck") supports O(1) insertion and removal at **both** ends. It can act as a stack, a queue, or both at once.

For a deque holding n items:

| Python `collections.deque` | Cost |
|---|---|
| `append(x)`, `appendleft(x)` | O(1) |
| `pop()`, `popleft()` | O(1) |
| `d[0]`, `d[-1]` | O(1) |
| `d[i]` in the middle | O(n) |

```python
from collections import deque
d = deque([2, 3])
d.appendleft(1)   # [1, 2, 3]
d.append(4)       # [1, 2, 3, 4]
d.popleft()       # 1
d.pop()           # 4
```

How it's built varies:

- **CPython's `deque`** is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks (64 items each), so both ends are O(1) with no resizing, and access near the middle is O(n). Its docs note that appends and pops from either end are thread-safe.
- **Java's `ArrayDeque`** is a growable circular array. It's the recommended general-purpose queue and stack in Java, and usually faster than `LinkedList`.
- **C++'s `std::deque`** is typically implemented as an array of pointers to fixed-size chunks. The standard guarantees constant-time indexing (random-access iterators) as well as constant-time insertion and removal at both ends.

### Bounded deques

`deque(maxlen=n)` keeps only the most recent n items. Appending to a full one silently discards an item from the **opposite** end. It's perfect for "the last 100 log lines" or a moving average.

```python
recent = deque(maxlen=3)
for x in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    recent.append(x)
# Keeps only the three newest values.
# deque([3, 4, 5], maxlen=3)
print(recent)
```

### A bounded history differs from a bounded work queue

A deque with a positive maxlen is an eviction policy: a full append removes the oldest item at the opposite end. It does not wait for a consumer to make room. A Queue with maxsize is a coordination policy: a blocking put waits when the queue is full.

For the five successive values one through five and a three-item history, the retained values are three, four and five. Adding zero at the left then discards five at the right, leaving zero, three and four. Choose maxlen for recent context that may be discarded, rather than work items that must all be processed.

Thread-safe individual deque appends and pops do not make a multi-step check-then-pop protocol atomic. Between checking nonemptiness and popping, another thread could remove the last item. Use a coordinating queue or an explicit lock when several operations form one protocol.

## Key takeaways
- A deque supports both ends; its middle-access cost depends on implementation.
- A maxlen history evicts from the opposite end instead of blocking producers.

## Further reading
- [Double-ended queue — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-ended_queue)
- [collections.deque — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)
- [ArrayDeque — Java SE 21 API](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/ArrayDeque.html)

lessons.title: A FIFO frontier finds unweighted distances
lessons.summary: Enqueue newly discovered nodes once and record their distance immediately.
lessons.body:
A FIFO queue processes older discoveries before newer ones. That order gives shortest edge-count distances in an unweighted graph. Use the deque import shown below; each neighbour in the example must also be a key in the adjacency mapping.

## Queues in BFS

**Breadth-first search** explores a graph in rings: all nodes one edge away, then two, then three. A queue enforces exactly that order, because nodes discovered earlier (closer) are processed before nodes discovered later (further).

```python
from collections import deque

def bfs(graph, start):
    dist = {start: 0}
    q = deque([start])
    while q:
        # Process the oldest discovered
        # node.
        node = q.popleft()
        for nb in graph[node]:
            if nb not in dist:
                # Mark discovery before
                # enqueueing.
                dist[nb] = dist[node] + 1
                q.append(nb)
    return dist
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Ripples from a stone
> Drop a stone in a still pond and the ripples spread outwards in rings: everything one step away is reached before anything two steps away.
>
> **How it maps:** The stone is `start`, each ring is one more edge of distance, and the queue holds the expanding front of the ripple. Because the queue serves older discoveries first, the whole of one ring is processed before the next ring begins.
>
> **Where it stops:** Ripples spread continuously and in every direction at once, while BFS processes one node at a time and only along edges. The ring picture also assumes every edge has the same length; weighted graphs need a different algorithm.

In an **unweighted graph**, `dist` is the shortest number of edges from `start` to every reachable node. Replacing the queue with a stack removes the shortest-path guarantee. With discovery marked on push, it is a LIFO traversal but does not necessarily reproduce recursive DFS discovery/parent order; standard DFS uses an appropriate marking or iterator-stack strategy. Graph traversal gets a full treatment in the graphs module.

> [!warning] Mark nodes when you enqueue them
> Mark a node as seen when it's **added** to the queue, not when it's removed. Otherwise the same node can be enqueued many times by different neighbours, blowing up time and memory on dense graphs.

### Two routes to the same node

Suppose A discovers B and C; both lead to D, while C also leads to E. D and E both lead to F. Starting at A, the queue processes A, B, C, D, E, F when neighbours are listed in that order.

D is marked when B enqueues it, so C does not enqueue it again. F is similarly discovered once. Its shortest distance is three edges: the queue has processed every one-edge and two-edge discovery before a three-edge node can be removed.

This claim depends on equal edge cost. A weighted edge cannot be represented merely by one queue step; weighted shortest paths require another strategy. The returned mapping covers only reachable nodes, and a missing adjacency key raises KeyError in this compact teaching implementation. Graph representation, traversal complexity and weighted shortest paths are explored in later modules.

## Key takeaways
- Enqueue newly discovered nodes once and record their distance immediately.
- FIFO exploration processes reachable nodes in nondecreasing unweighted distance.

## Further reading
- [collections.deque — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html)
- [Breadth-first search — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadth-first_search)
